items.title: A secrets scanner wore 16 AI crawler names: 358 requests for .env files, none for a page
items.summary: In 39 hours of our public bot log, one hosting network sent GPTBot, ClaudeBot, Googlebot and 13 other names after .env, .git/config and Firebase keys. The network gives it away; the TLS fingerprint does not. A 26-line check.
items.content_html:
A crawler's user agent (the name a program gives itself in each request) is a claim anyone can type. Our public bot log for motdang.net 1 shows what that costs. Between 01:39 UTC on 26 November and 16:59 UTC on 27 November 2026, one small hosting network sent 358 requests under 16 AI and search crawler names: GPTBot, ClaudeBot, Googlebot, PerplexityBot, Applebot and eleven more. Not one asked for a page. It asked for .env, .git/config, firebase-admin-key.json and 81 other places where an app stores its keys.

The log is a day-by-day file of every request the site's classifier does not count as a person, published under CC BY 4.0 1. Since 26 November each row carries the caller's network, its TLS fingerprint and its round-trip time; it has no addresses 2. Counts below are weighted: the log stores one row in N when the site is busy and says so in each row's weight 2. On the scanner's rows the weight was 1 to 4. Measured 28 November 2026 with DuckDB over the files for 26 and 27 November.

84 secret paths, 16 names, eight bursts

The scanner came from one network number (an ASN, the number that identifies who routes a block of internet addresses): AS214481, registered with RIPE NCC, the registry for Europe 3. Every request entered Cloudflare in Amsterdam. It came in eight bursts three to nine hours apart, 17 to 55 requests each, a minute or two long, each burst rotating through the names.

Path asked forRequestsNames used for it
/settings.json134
/.env.example124
/secrets.json102
/api/v1/env103
/api/env104
/.git/config94
/firebase-config.json94
/.aws/credentials, /actuator/heapdump, /debug/pprof/cmdline3 to 7 each2 to 4

Our site answered 266 of the 358 with 404 and 91 with a redirect to a page of text; the one 200 was /sw.js, the public service worker file every visitor downloads.

The list reads like a map of what AI-built apps publish by mistake: a .env file copied into the build folder, a Firebase admin key in public/, a .git folder on a static host. A scanner that dresses as GPTBot is betting that a site lets AI crawlers past rules that stop everyone else.

For six names, every request in the log was the scanner

Some of the names it wore have no owner sending them. Google says Google-Extended is a robots.txt token only and has no user agent string of its own 4. Anthropic lists three bots, ClaudeBot, Claude-User and Claude-SearchBot 5; anthropic-ai and Claude-Web are not among them.

NameAll requestsFrom the scanner
Googlebot4228
PerplexityBot5929
ChatGPT-User32822
ClaudeBot1,06228
Applebot2,10012
GPTBot98,03911

On a small site, two in three requests named Googlebot were the scanner. A dashboard that counts user agents reports an AI crawler visiting; the log shows a key hunt.

The network tells them apart; the TLS fingerprint does not

The crawlers with an owner arrive from that owner's network:

  • GPTBot: 98,026 of 98,039 requests from Microsoft's AS8075. OpenAI publishes GPTBot's addresses 67; we looked up 3 of its 18 address blocks at RIPEstat today, and all three sit in AS8075.
  • ClaudeBot: 1,032 of 1,062 from addresses registered to Anthropic, PBC.
  • Applebot: 2,088 of 2,100 from Apple's AS714. Apple verifies Applebot by reverse DNS or its published address list 8.

A TLS fingerprint is a hash of the encryption options a program offers when it connects; Cloudflare gives it to a Worker as tlsClientCiphersSha1 9. It names the software library, and libraries are shared. The scanner used five fingerprints. All five also appear on 2,832 requests named Bytespider from Amazon's Singapore network in the same 39 hours. A fingerprint narrows the field; the network separates the scanner from the crawler.

A 26-line check in a Cloudflare Worker

A Cloudflare Worker (a small program that runs in front of a site) reads the caller's network number from request.cf.asn on every plan 9. The check below answers 404 when a request names a listed crawler from a network that crawler does not use, or uses a name its owner does not list:

// Crawler name → networks (ASNs) its owner crawls from, per our log.
const OWNERS = {
  GPTBot: [8075], "OAI-SearchBot": [8075], "ChatGPT-User": [8075],
  ClaudeBot: [16509], Applebot: [714], Googlebot: [15169],
  bingbot: [8075], "meta-externalagent": [32934], Amazonbot: [14618, 16509],
};
// Names their owners do not list as a user agent.
const RETIRED = ["anthropic-ai", "Claude-Web", "Google-Extended"];

export function check(ua, asn) {
  if (RETIRED.some((n) => ua.includes(n))) return "retired name";
  for (const [name, nets] of Object.entries(OWNERS)) {
    if (ua.includes(name)) return nets.includes(asn) ? "ok" : "wrong network";
  }
  return "not a listed crawler";
}

export default {
  async fetch(request) {
    const verdict = check(request.headers.get("user-agent") || "", request.cf?.asn);
    if (verdict === "wrong network" || verdict === "retired name") {
      return new Response("Not found", { status: 404 });
    }
    return fetch(request);
  },
};

Tested today with Node against seven user agent and network pairs from the log: 7 of 7 verdicts as expected. A network check is coarse. Anyone renting a server on Microsoft's cloud can claim GPTBot from AS8075, and Amazon's AS16509 carries thousands of customers besides Anthropic. The finer check is the address itself against the owner's published list 7 or, for Google, reverse DNS 10; a check by network is the cheap first cut.

The paths it hunts are a test for your own site

The scanner's list doubles as a checklist. Ask your own site for the same files; each answer other than 404 or a redirect to a page needs a look:

for p in .env .env.production .git/config firebase-config.json firebase-admin-key.json \
         secrets.json settings.json config.json .aws/credentials api/env; do
  printf '%s %s\n' "$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://example.com/$p")" "$p"
done

A 200 on .env or a Firebase admin key means the key is public. The fix is in two places: rotate the key at its provider, then remove the file from the folder the host publishes. The scanner came back eight times in the 39 hours on record.

items.title: Llama 3.3 and gpt-oss on Workers AI get a date you did not send, a day behind in Thailand
items.summary: Three of nine models we asked on Workers AI read a date line the caller did not write. At 06:48 in Bangkok all three said 26 November; gpt-oss-20b still did at 07:05. A date in your own system prompt won 5 times of 5.
items.content_html:
At 06:48 in Bangkok on 27 November 2026 we asked Llama 3.3 70B on Cloudflare Workers AI "What is today's date?", with no system prompt (the instructions an app sends before the user's message). It answered "November 26, 2026", five times of five. Asked to repeat any line above the question that names a date, it printed two lines that were not in our request: Cutting Knowledge Date: December 2023 and Today Date: 26 Nov 2026. gpt-oss-20b and gpt-oss-120b printed Current date: 2026-11-26. A paper posted on 17 October 2026 calls this date the hidden variable in model testing 1. For a shop bot in Thailand it is also a wrong answer for the first seven hours of every day.

Three of nine models get a date line from the template

A chat template is the code shipped with a model that turns a list of messages into the text the model reads. Meta's documented format for Llama 3.1 and 3.3 starts every system turn with a knowledge-cutoff line and a Today Date: line 23. OpenAI's Harmony format for gpt-oss puts Knowledge cutoff: and Current date: in a system message the caller does not write 4. On Workers AI the template runs on Cloudflare's side, so the app never sees these lines.

We asked nine models on Workers AI to repeat any line above our question that mentions a date or a knowledge cutoff, once with no system prompt and once with "You are a helpful assistant.":

Model on Workers AILine it repeated, 06:44 to 06:50 BangkokSame with our own system prompt
Llama 3.3 70B fp8 fastToday Date: 26 Nov 2026yes
gpt-oss-20bCurrent date: 2026-11-26yes
gpt-oss-120bCurrent date: 2026-11-26yes
Llama 4 Scout, Mistral Small 3.1, Granite 4.0 H Micro, DeepSeek V4.1 FlashNONENONE
Qwen 3.8 27BNONEempty reply
Gemma 4 26Bempty replyempty reply

Sending your own system prompt does not remove the line on these three; the template adds it above yours.

The line follows a clock that is not Thailand's

We asked again at 07:01 Bangkok, one minute after midnight UTC. Llama 3.3 and gpt-oss-120b now said 27 November. gpt-oss-20b still said Current date: 2026-11-26 at 07:05, in 9 of 9 answers that named a date from 07:01 to 07:05. Llama 3.3 and gpt-oss-120b follow a UTC calendar; which clock gpt-oss-20b follows is unknown.

So between 00:00 and 07:00 in Thailand, a Llama 3.3 or gpt-oss-120b bot with no date of its own tells a customer it is yesterday, and gpt-oss-20b was still a day behind past 07:00. "Days left until 1 January 2027?" got 36 in 4 of the 10 gpt-oss answers before 07:00; the answer in Bangkok was 35.

Models without the line make a date up

Four of the models with no hidden date line answered "What is today's date?" like this, five times each, before and after 07:00:

ModelToday's date, no system promptDays to 1 January 2027
Granite 4.0 H Micro"August 1, 2021""1,000", as of October 2021
Llama 4 Scout"5/10/2024"996
Mistral Small 3.1declines1,359, as of 10 October 2023
DeepSeek V4.1 Flashdeclines450, assuming 8 October 2025, in 7 of 10; 442 or 507 in the rest

Llama 3.3, which had the right date in its hidden line after 07:00, still answered 364 and before 07:00 365: it read the date for the first question and ignored it for the arithmetic.

Your own date line wins, in your customer's time zone

With the system prompt "You are a helpful assistant for a shop in Chiang Rai. Today's date is 27 November 2026." all seven models that gave an answer said "27 November 2026", 5 times of 5 in each run, including the three whose template said 26 November. Days to 1 January 2027:

gpt-oss-120b said 35 five times before 07:00 and 34 five times after. gpt-oss-20b said 34 in 9 of 10. Granite said 31 in 10 of 10. Date arithmetic belongs in code; the model gets the result.

A Worker (Cloudflare's server code) that writes the date in the customer's time zone with Intl.DateTimeFormat and its timeZone option 8:

const today = new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-GB", {
  timeZone: "Asia/Bangkok", weekday: "long", day: "numeric", month: "long", year: "numeric",
}).format(new Date());
const daysToNewYear = Math.round(
  (Date.UTC(2027, 0, 1) - Date.parse(new Date().toLocaleDateString("en-CA", { timeZone: "Asia/Bangkok" }))) / 86400000);

const messages = [
  { role: "system", content: `You answer for a shop in Chiang Rai. Today is ${today} (Thailand time). Days until 1 January 2027: ${daysToNewYear}.` },
  { role: "user", content: userText },
];
const reply = await env.AI.run("@cf/meta/llama-3.3-70b-instruct-fp8-fast", { messages });

In testing, the hidden date changed less than the server's own noise

The paper ran six open models on their own machines at greedy decoding (the model takes its single likeliest word each time) and reran with only the date changed. Two dates between 2024 and 2026 moved a median 6.6% of test items between right and wrong, and moving the date by one day moved 4.3% 1. With the date and setup fixed, its reruns reproduced byte for byte 1. None of the eleven testing tools it audited pins the date 1.

On Workers AI we cannot pin it, so we ran 100 arithmetic word problems through Llama 3.3 70B three times before 07:00 (hidden date 26 November) and twice after (27 November), temperature 0. Each run scored 98 or 99 of 100. Between two runs on the same date, 1 or 2 items switched between right and wrong; between runs on different dates, 0 to 3. The text of the answer differed in 61 to 90 of 100 items between any two runs, same date or not. Temperature 0 on a shared server does not give the same text twice here, so the date's effect on this test is smaller than we can see.

For anyone comparing models on Workers AI: run each test at least twice on the same day before reading a difference between models, and write the date and time of the run next to the score.

How we measured

From Chiang Rai on 27 November 2026, through Workers AI's OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint: @cf/meta/llama-3.3-70b-instruct-fp8-fast 5, @cf/openai/gpt-oss-20b 6, @cf/openai/gpt-oss-120b 7, @cf/meta/llama-4-scout-17b-16e-instruct, @cf/mistralai/mistral-small-3.1-24b-instruct, @cf/ibm-granite/granite-4.0-h-micro, @cf/deepseek-ai/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017, @cf/qwen/qwen3.8-27b and @cf/google/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it, temperature 0. The date questions allowed 60 output tokens, 1,500 for gpt-oss, whose reasoning comes first. Each date question ran five times per model and system prompt, at 06:48 to 06:50 and 07:02 to 07:05 Bangkok time.

The 100 word problems are ours, generated with fixed numbers: packing, discounts, clock times, sums across stalls, floor tiles. The answer is the last number in the reply; Llama 3.3 got 400 output tokens to work. Two runs at 06:45 to 06:47 with a 16-token limit were dropped: the model wrote working, not a number. The whole run used under US$0.40 of Workers AI time at the listed prices 567.

Hongdam builds chat assistants on Workers AI, LINE and models you run yourself 9.

items.title: n8n 2.50 retries a failed trigger 25 times in 72 hours; its crash shut-off is off
items.summary: n8n 2.50.0 and 3.4.0, pre-releases from 24 November, bring a trigger back after an outage without a re-publish; stable 2.49.6 does not. Unpublishing a workflow that crashes n8n is off unless you set one variable.
items.content_html:
A trigger is the first node of an n8n workflow: the webhook, mail inbox, schedule or poll that starts each run. When you publish a workflow, n8n registers its triggers with the outside service. If that service is down at that moment, or n8n restarts during its outage, activation fails. On n8n 2.49.6, the stable release on 26 November 2026 3, the workflow stays published with a dead trigger until someone publishes it again; the change that ends this says it lets a workflow "recover without a user publishing it again" 4.

That change, PR #43708, merged on 20 November and shipped on 24 November in two pre-releases: 2.50.0 and 3.4.0 124. A pre-release is the version n8n puts out for testing before it becomes the default download. The same releases carry a second change, PR #43685, which unpublishes a workflow that crashes the whole n8n process 6. On a self-hosted instance that one is off by default 78.

A failed trigger now retries on a doubling clock for three days

The schedule lives in three constants in the 3.4.0 source 5: the first retry waits one minute, each failed retry doubles the wait, the wait stops growing at four hours, and retries end once a trigger has failed for three days. The comments give the reasons: a retry at once would hit the same outage, a four-hour cap limits a dead trigger to six attempts a day, and three days covers an outage from Friday evening to Monday morning 5.

We replayed those rules in a short script on 26 November 2026, with each attempt taking no time; real times run a few seconds later.

RetryWait before itTime since the first failure
11 min1 min
22 min3 min
34 min7 min
48 min15 min
516 min31 min
632 min1 h 03 min
764 min2 h 07 min
8128 min4 h 15 min
9 to 254 h each8 h 15 min to 72 h 15 min

The cost of the cap: after the first eight hours, a service that comes back waits up to four hours for its trigger. An inbox server that returns at 8 h 20 min gets its trigger back at the 12 h 15 min retry, 3 h 55 min later. A restart of n8n, or a new leader in a multi-main setup, tries every scheduled workflow once without waiting for its delay 4, so a restart is the quick way to bring one back.

Three more details from the PR 4:

  • A failure that needs a person (a policy refusal, two workflows on the same webhook path) schedules no retry.
  • Publishing by hand resets the schedule and gives the trigger the usual five activation attempts.
  • The database migration schedules a first retry for failures already on record, so a dead trigger from last week gets its first try after the upgrade.

During a rolling upgrade, failures recorded by a leader still on the older version get no delay and stay unscheduled 4.

The crash shut-off counts three crashes in six hours, and is off unless you turn it on

n8n already marks runs that were in progress at a crash as crashed, and it can unpublish a workflow whose last three runs crashed, then email the owner. PR #43685 lists four ways a crash loop slipped past that check 6. Two of them: a workflow set not to save failed runs loses its crashed rows at the next pruning, and a poll trigger crashing n8n mid-fetch leaves no run at all.

The fix writes a small file next to n8n's crash log. At each start after a crash, if exactly one workflow was in progress, that workflow gets one crash on its tally; if none or several were, the tally clears. Crashes older than six hours drop out. At three, n8n unpublishes the workflow before the scheduler starts any job 6.

The PR states the feature is on in n8n Cloud 6. Self-hosted, both the old check and the new tally read one setting 79, and the docs list its default as false 8. With it off, n8n logs a warning naming the workflow that was alone in flight at the crash, and leaves it published 9.

Turning it on

Two environment variables control it 8:

N8N_WORKFLOW_AUTODEACTIVATION_ENABLED=true
# crashes in a row, within six hours, before the workflow is unpublished; 3 is the default
N8N_WORKFLOW_AUTODEACTIVATION_MAX_LAST_EXECUTIONS=3

Set them where n8n gets its environment: the environment: block of a Docker Compose file, or the service's environment file. The crash tally needs 2.50.0 or 3.4.0 12; on 2.49.6 the variable turns on only the older last-three-runs check.

For an install on 2.x, 2.50.0 carries both changes without the move to the 3.x line 12. On 2.49.6, a trigger that failed activation during an outage waits for someone to publish the workflow again 4.

items.title: Drupal's install.php flaw is exploited; an exact-match block let /install.php/foo through
items.summary: CISA lists the Drupal installer flaw as exploited, deadline 27 November. Drupal 11.4.13 changes four things in the installer. On Apache, a rule matching only the exact path let /core/install.php/foo through.
items.content_html:
Drupal published SA-CORE-2026-017 on 18 November 2026, rated Highly critical, 20 of 25 1. An attacker who reaches /core/install.php, Drupal's setup script, can under some conditions make it run again over a site that is already installed. The result is a site takeover or remote code execution (the attacker runs their own code on your server) 1. The advisory's update says attacks on live sites began by 19 November, 19:00 UTC 1. CISA added CVE-2026-132165 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog (the US list of flaws attackers are using) on 24 November, with a due date of 27 November for US federal agencies 23. The advisory credits Anthropic's open-source scanner with finding it 1.

BranchFixed inStatus
Drupal 11.4.x11.4.13supported
Drupal 11.3.x11.3.22supported
Drupal 10.6.x10.6.22supported
Drupal 11.2.x and older, 10.5.x and older, 8, 9no fixend of life

A site on an end-of-life branch gets no patch 1. Blocking the installer, below, is the step that covers it.

The fix changes four things in the installer

We downloaded the 11.4.12 and 11.4.13 release files from Drupal.org and compared them 56. Outside version numbers and bundled libraries, three files in core changed; the installer changes are in core/includes/install.core.inc. The same changes are present in 10.6.22 and 11.3.22 (measured 25 November 2026, by searching each release's copy of that file for the new code).

  1. A failed database check now stops the installer. Before, install_verify_database_ready() caught any error while checking for an existing install and carried on as if the database were empty. The comment said the database "might not be set up yet". Now the error throws, and the installer reports that the configured database could not be verified 6. CISA files the flaw under CWE-636, "not failing securely" 3: the old code treated an error as permission.
  2. A finished install now refuses to restart. The installer reads its last completed task and the install_time value, which Drupal writes when installation finishes. If either says the site is done, it throws AlreadyInstalledException 6.
  3. Only the first browser can continue. The installer now stores a random token in the session of the first browser to reach the full start-up, and a hash of it in the database. A different browser gets "Access denied" 6.
  4. The installer stops changing file permissions on settings.php. Drupal's file check used to try chmod() on settings.php to make it writable whenever the web server owned the file. Every call in the installer now passes auto_fix: FALSE 6. This matches the advisory's note that some attack paths fail when the web server cannot write to or change permissions on settings.php 1.

The other two changed files harden cache classes against PHP object injection, where an attacker feeds the site crafted serialized data that rebuilds objects of their choosing: YamlCacheCollectorDiscovery now refuses to be unserialized, and CacheCollector checks the type of its cache and lock objects before writing 6. The 11.4.13 package also updates the bundled Guzzle HTTP library to 7.16.3, whose changelog lists two security fixes of its own 6.

Block install.php: the prefix and file rules blocked all six forms, the exact-match rule missed one

Drupal's documentation, updated 21 November, says to block the installer once a site is installed, and gives three ways 4. It warns against an exact-match rule in Nginx, because servers that send any URL containing .php/ to PHP will still run /core/install.php/foo 4. The extra part after the file name is called path info, and PHP runs the file with it.

We tested the Apache versions of those rules on 25 November 2026: Apache 2.4.67, the unmodified Drupal 11.4.13 tree with its own .htaccess, AcceptPathInfo On to stand in for a PHP handler, 10 URLs per rule, one request each, 40 in all. A 200 means the installer file was served.

URLNo rule<Location>.htaccess <Files>Exact <LocationMatch>
/core/install.php200403403403
/core/install.php/foo200403403200
/core/install.php?profile=standard200403403403
/core//install.php200403403403
/core/./install.php200403403403
/core/%69nstall.php200403403403
/install.php301301403301
/index.php, /update.php, /core/rebuild.php200200200200

The exact rule, <LocationMatch "^/core/install\.php$">, blocked the plain path and let path info through: the same gap Drupal describes for Nginx 4. <Location "/core/install.php"> caught it, because Apache applies a Location to any URL that starts with the location plus a slash 7. The 301 on /install.php is Drupal's own .htaccess sending visitors to /core/install.php, where the block answers. The site, update.php (database updates) and rebuild.php answered 200 under every rule.

Apache's documentation gives one more reason to prefer a file rule: several URLs can reach the same file, so a URL-based rule should not carry access control alone 7. A <Files "install.php"> rule matches the file whatever URL reached it.

What to run today

Update first, to the release for your branch in the table above 1, and run drush updatedb or /update.php 4. Then block the installer. In Apache's server configuration, for every virtual host that serves the site 4:

<Location "/core/install.php">
  Require all denied
</Location>

On shared hosting, add a <Files "install.php"> block with Require all denied to the .htaccess in the web root 4. Composer rewrites that .htaccess on every composer install, so a hand edit disappears; Drupal's page shows the drupal-scaffold append setting that re-adds it each time 4. In Nginx, use the prefix form, location ^~ /core/install.php { return 404; }, not location = 4.

Then check from outside:

curl -sI https://example.com/core/install.php     | head -1
curl -sIL https://example.com/install.php         | grep HTTP
curl -sI https://example.com/core/install.php/foo | head -1

All three should end in 403 or 404 4. A 200 on any of them means the installer still answers.

CISA marks this entry for forensic triage 3. A site that was reachable and unpatched after 19 November has a reason to look for signs of a reinstall: a changed settings.php, admin accounts nobody made, or a fresh install_time value in the key_value table.

items.title: Vercel's 20 MiB uploads need 4 GB of memory; Next.js Server Actions still stop at 1 MB
items.summary: Vercel raised the request body limit from 4.5 MB to 20 MiB on 20 November, in beta. It takes three switches and a paid plan, and the Edge runtime keeps the old limit. A photo sent as base64 JSON loses a quarter of the room.
items.content_html:
An upload form on a Vercel app fails above 4.5 MB with a 413, the HTTP code for "payload too large". On 20 November 2026 Vercel raised that ceiling to 20 MiB (20,971,520 bytes) as a public beta 1. The new limit is off until a project turns on three settings, one of them only on paid plans, and it does nothing for the 1 MB limits that Next.js sets on its own.

Three switches, and the Hobby plan has no way in

Vercel's limits page, read today, lists the steps 2:

  1. Fluid compute on. Fluid compute is Vercel's newer way of running functions, where one instance serves several requests at once. It is on by default for projects created since 23 April 2025 9; older projects turn it on in Settings or with "fluid": true in vercel.json.
  2. Function memory set to Performance, 4 GB with 2 vCPUs. The memory page says this is set in the dashboard under Settings, Functions, and not in vercel.json 3.
  3. An environment variable, then a redeploy:
vercel env add VERCEL_SUPPORT_LARGE_REQUEST_BODY preview
# value: 1
vercel deploy

The variable works per environment, so Preview can try it before Production 1.

The limits page gives Hobby a maximum of 2 GB of memory; Pro and Enterprise go to 4 GB 2. A Hobby project cannot meet step 2, so it stays at 4.5 MB.

The beta covers the Node.js, Python and Bun runtimes 2. A function or Routing Middleware on the Edge runtime stays at 4.5 MB and answers 413; the changelog's fix is runtime: 'nodejs' on the route 1. Responses stay at 4.5 MB unless streamed 2.

Middleware stops seeing the body

With the variable set, Routing Middleware (code that runs before every request reaches its route) receives the headers and no body, for the whole project 1. Vercel's reason is to avoid sending a 20 MiB body twice 1. Middleware that reads the body, such as a webhook signature check or a bot filter that inspects a form, stops working on the first deploy with the flag. The check moves into the route handler, which still gets the full body.

Performance memory doubles one line of the bill

Vercel bills functions on fluid compute by Active CPU, Provisioned Memory and invocations 3. Provisioned Memory is charged per GB-hour while an instance is up. The pricing page's rate for the Washington D.C. region, read today, is US$0.0106 per GB-hour 4. At 2 GB an instance-hour costs US$0.0212 in memory; at 4 GB, US$0.0424. The setting applies to every function in the project, not only the upload route 3. Twice the CPU can shorten CPU-bound work, which offsets part of it 3.

A base64 JSON upload fits 3.37 MB, multipart fits 4.50 MB

The limit counts the request body, not the file. Apps that AI tools write often read the file in the browser, turn it into base64 text (a way of writing bytes as letters, which takes 4 characters for every 3 bytes) and post it inside JSON. A multipart form, the browser's own way of sending a file, adds a few hundred bytes.

Measured 24 November 2026 on a local server that reports each body's length: random files from 1 MB to 16 MB, posted with curl once as multipart (-F file=@…) and once as JSON carrying a data:image/jpeg;base64,… string. Every multipart body was the file plus 195 bytes. Every JSON body was 1.3333 times the file plus 52 bytes.

FileMultipart bodyBase64 JSON bodyUnder 4.5 MB?Under 20 MiB?
3,000,000 bytes3,000,1954,000,052bothboth
3,400,000 bytes3,400,1954,533,388multipart onlyboth
4,400,000 bytes4,400,1955,866,720multipart onlyboth
15,000,000 bytes15,000,19520,000,052neitherboth
16,000,000 bytes16,000,19521,333,388neithermultipart only

From those overheads, the largest file each way fits:

Sending the file as multipart (FormData in the browser) buys a third more room under either limit, with no Vercel setting changed.

Next.js sets 1 MB of its own

Vercel's limit is the outer wall. Next.js has two inner ones, from its docs read today:

Where the upload landsNext.js defaultRaised with
A Server Action (a function the form calls directly, App Router)1 MB 6experimental.serverActions.bodySizeLimit in next.config.js
A Pages Router API route1 MB 7export const config = { api: { bodyParser: { sizeLimit: '20mb' } } }
// next.config.js
module.exports = {
  experimental: {
    serverActions: { bodySizeLimit: '20mb' },
  },
}

The Server Actions page counts multipart boundaries in the limit and suggests 10 to 20 KB of room over the largest file 6. An app that sets Vercel's flag and leaves these alone fails at 1 MB with a Next.js error, not Vercel's 413.

Larger files skip the function

Vercel's error page for FUNCTION_PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE lists the other routes: compress, split, or upload straight to storage 5. With Vercel Blob, upload() from @vercel/blob/client sends the file from the browser to the store, and a small route running handleUpload() hands out the token 8. The body never passes through a function, so neither limit applies. The client-upload page says the route that issues tokens has to check who is asking, or anyone can fill the store 8.

Which to use

  • Under 3.37 MB as JSON or 4.5 MB as multipart: nothing to change.
  • Up to 20 MiB, on Pro, with no body-reading middleware: the three switches, plus the Next.js limit raised to match.
  • On Hobby, past 20 MiB, or with middleware that reads bodies: upload to storage from the browser.

Finding which of these an AI-written app needs, and wiring it, is part of the last-mile work we sell 10.

items.title: Workers AI retired 16 models on 20 November: 14 answer 410, two still reply
items.summary: We called each retired model on 23 November. Fourteen fail on every call with error code 5028, streamed or not. Llama 3.2 3B and Gemma 2B LoRA answered 14 of 14. A check that needs no token, and a spare model in the call.
items.content_html:
Cloudflare's Workers AI retired 16 language models on 20 November 2026 1. On 23 November we called each of them four times through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Fourteen answered HTTP 410 with error code 5028 on 56 of 56 calls, in a median of 0.15 seconds. Two answered every call with a normal reply: @cf/meta/llama-3.2-3b-instruct and @cf/google/gemma-2b-it-lora, 14 of 14 each, though both pages read "Deprecated 11/20/2026" 34.

An app that names one of the fourteen has failed on every model call since 20 November. The notice gives the date and no hour 1.

The refusal names the model and the date

HTTP 410 is the web's status for a thing removed on purpose. The body for a retired model:

{"errors":[{"message":"AiError: Model has been deprecated: @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3-flash was deprecated on 2026-11-20. See the model catalog for alternatives: https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers-ai/models/ (…request id…)","code":5028}],"success":false,"result":{},"messages":[]}
Model id sentHTTP statusError codeCallsSeconds
One of 14 retired ids410502856 of 560.15 median, 0.12 to 0.44
Llama 3.2 3B, Gemma 2B LoRA (retired)200none28 of 280.23 to 1.33
An invented id, a misspelt id40050073 of 30.18 to 1.16

Both codes match Cloudflare's error table: 5028 "Model deprecated" with 410, 5007 "No such model" with 400 2. A retired id and a typing mistake get different answers, so a log line can tell them apart.

With "stream": true (the reply sent word by word), the 410 came as the HTTP status with the same JSON body, before any stream opened: 14 of 14. Code that checks the status before reading the stream catches it.

The OpenAI client libraries retry connection errors and statuses 408, 409, 429 and 500 and above, twice by default 6. 410 is outside that list, so the first call raises the error. An app that catches every error and prints "try again later" now prints it on every request, and the cause sits in the log.

Two retired models still answer

ModelCalls answeredTime span, BangkokDocs page
@cf/meta/llama-3.2-3b-instruct14 of 1410:13 to 10:18Deprecated 11/20/2026 3
@cf/google/gemma-2b-it-lora14 of 1410:13 to 10:18Deprecated 11/20/2026 4

The replies carried text and a usage block with token counts. Both models accept LoRA adapters (small add-on weights from fine-tuning). So do gemma-7b-it-lora, llama-2-7b-chat-hf-lora and qwq-32b, which returned 410, so the adapter flag does not explain it. The notice lists both among the 16 and names no exception 1. The cause is unknown, and so is the day they stop. We called from one account in Thailand.

All 16 model pages show "Deprecated" and the date, and the pricing page still lists retired models with their prices 5. A price on that page is not a sign that a model answers.

Find retired ids without a token

The docs serve each model page as plain text at …/models/<name>/index.md. This script lists every Workers AI id in a project and reads its page:

grep -rhoE '@(cf|hf)/[A-Za-z0-9._/-]+' . --include='*.js' --include='*.ts' --include='*.py' \
  --include='*.toml' --include='*.json' --include='*.jsonc' --exclude-dir=node_modules | sort -u |
while read -r id; do
  page="https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers-ai/models/${id##*/}/index.md"
  when=$(curl -s "$page" | grep -m1 -oE 'Deprecated[^0-9]{0,12}[0-9]{1,2}/[0-9]{1,2}/[0-9]{4}')
  echo "${when:-in service or no page}  $id"
done

Run on a test file with four ids on 23 November 2026:

in service or no page  @cf/google/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it
Deprecated | 11/20/2026  @cf/meta/llama-3.2-3b-instruct
Deprecated | 11/20/2026  @cf/moonshotai/kimi-k2.6
Deprecated | 11/20/2026  @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3-flash

Ids stored in a dashboard variable or a database are outside its reach. Pages showed the date before 20 November too: our 20 November note read the Llama 3.2 pages as listed for retirement that day. Run weekly, the script reports the next round while its date is still ahead.

A spare model in the call

import json, os, urllib.request, urllib.error

URL = f"https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/{os.environ['CF_ACCOUNT_ID']}/ai/v1/chat/completions"
TOKEN = os.environ["CF_API_TOKEN"]
MODELS = ["@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3-flash", "@cf/google/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it"]   # first choice, then the spare

def ask(prompt):
    for model in MODELS:
        body = {"model": model, "max_tokens": 200, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]}
        req = urllib.request.Request(URL, json.dumps(body).encode(),
                                     {"Authorization": f"Bearer {TOKEN}", "Content-Type": "application/json"})
        try:
            reply = json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=120))
            return model, reply["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]
        except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
            errors = json.loads(e.read() or b"{}").get("errors") or [{}]
            if e.code == 410 and errors[0].get("code") == 5028:
                print("RETIRED:", errors[0].get("message"))    # send this line to your alerts
                continue
            raise
    raise RuntimeError("every model in MODELS is retired")

Tested 23 November 2026 with the retired GLM-5.3 Flash first: it printed the RETIRED line and returned Gemma 4 26B's answer. The spare costs one extra call of about 0.15 seconds per request until someone edits the list. The spare is a different model, and its answers differ; our 9 November note measured the two small replacements on ten tasks 8.

Cloudflare's AI Gateway has the same idea without code: its Universal endpoint takes a list of steps and by default moves to the next when a model request returns an error 7. The page names no status codes, and we did not test it with a 410.

One named replacement took 11 to 54 seconds for one word

The notice names four models to move to 1. Each got the prompt "Reply with the one word: ok".

ReplacementCallsSeconds per call
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 101721.3, 1.0 (streamed)
GLM-5.311.0
Gemma 4 26B11.5
Qwen3.8 27B454.5, 28.4, 14.4, 11.5

Qwen3.8 27B wrote a line of reasoning (the working a model writes before its answer) and then "ok", 33 output tokens in the first call. Why that took 54 seconds is unknown; the four calls ran within four minutes and each was faster than the one before. A chat that moved to it on 20 November may feel slower for a reason outside the app's code. Time your own prompt before choosing.

How we measured

97 calls between 10:13 and 10:18 Bangkok time on 23 November 2026, through Workers AI's chat completions endpoint, one account, from Thailand. Each of the 16 retired ids: three plain calls and one streamed. The two that answered: ten more plain calls each. Five calls to the four replacements, three to two invented ids, three more to Qwen3.8 27B, and two for the spare-model test. The prompt asked for one word, with 40 output tokens allowed. Seconds are whole-call times from our machine. The 97 calls cost under US$0.01 at list prices 5. Not tested: the Workers binding (env.AI.run()), the /ai/run/ path, AI Gateway, and the eight retired image, speech and embedding models in the same notice 1. Hongdam moves an assistant to a new model by running the customer's own prompts on the candidates first 9.

items.title: The week: Ruby fixes seven memory flaws, Cloudflare versions expire, Supabase merge tokens
items.summary: Six notes, from a reasoning switch that still bills to a domain moved with one line. Plus five outside items: Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14, Cloudflare's 30-day version retention, and three billing and limit changes.
items.content_html:
Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14 came out on 18 November 2026 with fixes for seven memory flaws in two everyday operations: changing the case of a string and handling a regular expression (a search pattern) 1. The Ruby team writes that it knows of proofs of concept that reach remote code execution, an attacker running their own code on the server, for some of them 1. That leads the five outside items. First, the week's six notes.

Six notes, 16 to 21 November

Monday, models. Inkling 2 Small on Workers AI: reasoning_effort none still thinks, and bills for it: Cloudflare added Thinking Machines' open model on 12 November and said none turns reasoning off (reasoning is the working a model writes before its answer, billed as output). In 300 graded calls, none reasoned in 30 of 30 replies and used 16% more output tokens than the default. minimal got 30 of 30 right with 34% fewer tokens than the default. enable_thinking: false did switch reasoning off, and 19 of 30 answers were right.

Tuesday, last-mile. Supabase turned off four TLS 1.2 ciphers: 9 of 163 recorded clients now fail to connect: the removal announced for 10 November is in effect on project APIs. We replayed the opening message of 163 recorded browsers and runtimes. Safari 5 to 8, Chrome 30 and Opera 17 fail before they send a request, so nothing shows in the project's logs. IE 11 connects because one of the project's two certificates is ECDSA. Two openssl commands in the note test a project or a custom domain.

Wednesday, security. OpenSSH 10.6p2 shut the 300-byte password bypass on Alpine sshd: on Alpine Linux, a password 256 to 1,024 bytes long logged into accounts whose password field was *, the mark for a locked account. OpenSSH 10.6p2 of 5 November refuses the comparison, and CISA listed the flaw as exploited on 9 November. All eight Alpine branches we read carried the fixed package. PasswordAuthentication no closes the path without an upgrade.

Thursday, automation. n8n 2.48.4 and 2.47.7 stop blanking the execution page for a global credential: a run that used a global credential, one shared with every user of the installation, came back as "Data redacted" with no reveal button, even for the person who ran it. The fix shipped on 13 November in both lines and on 17 November in 2.49.0. Redaction set per workflow or by the instance works as before.

Friday, models. Order tickets from four open models: symbol codes silently wrong 186 times in 660, JSON 46: a paper from ITMO University reports that a ticket's format changes how often a small model writes a valid ticket for the wrong order. We prompted four models on Workers AI with 60 drink orders in four formats. Symbol codes did worst on all four models, JSON best. A short word check caught 28 of JSON's 46 silent errors, and Llama 4 Scout wrote 360 of 360 JSON tickets right.

Saturday, last-mile. One Cloudflare Pages line moved a domain: 147 of 147 URLs in one hop, POSTs become GETs: one _redirects line sends each old path and its query string to the new address. Without 301 at the end the line answers 302, the temporary code. A 301 turns a form's POST into a GET, so forms and webhooks need their own receiver. The note has a 16-line check and the conditions of Google's Change of Address tool.

Five items, 12 to 20 November

18 November: Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14. Six of the seven flaws are in the advisory as possible remote code execution; the seventh discloses memory or crashes the process 1. Two sit in case conversion, the code behind calls such as upcase and downcase: changing the case of a crafted string is the trigger 1. Four need an attacker-controlled pattern, as in a search box that accepts regular expressions 1. Affected: 3.3.13 and earlier, 3.4.0 to 3.4.12, 4.0.0 to 4.0.9; Ruby 3.2 and older get no fix 1. CVE numbers were requested and not yet assigned on the advisory, which uses GitHub advisory IDs 1. Cloudflare added two Ruby rules on 19 November, a heap overflow and an integer overflow, with the action Block in its Free and Managed rulesets 2. Docker Hub's record for the official ruby:4.0.10 image, read 22 November, is dated 19 November 00:49 UTC 3; the records for 3.4.13, 3.3.14, 4.0, 3.4 and latest carry the same date. A Dockerfile with FROM ruby:3.4 gets the fix on docker build --pull; one pinned to ruby:3.4.12 needs the new number. ruby -v prints the running version.

19 November: Cloudflare deletes Worker versions and Pages deployments after 30 days. A version is each upload of a Worker's code or change to its settings. After 30 days it goes, unless it is one of the 100 most recent or is deployed now 45. Pages follows the same count, with production and preview deployments counted together and the current production deployment exempt 6. A deleted version's Version URL stops working, as does a deleted Pages deployment's preview URL at <hash>.<project>.pages.dev 56. A preview link in an email to a client, a ticket or a slide is the casualty. Rollback reaches the 100 most recent Worker versions 5. For a link that lasts, Cloudflare points to Worker Previews, whose URL serves the latest deployment of that preview 4.

12 November: merging a Supabase branch needs a production token. A branch is a separate copy of a project for testing changes. Since 12 November, merging one into the main project needs a scoped personal access token with Production Branches: Read-write; a token with Development Branches access alone gets a permission error from the merge call and from the MCP merge_branch tool that AI agents use 7. Classic personal access tokens are unaffected 7. An existing token's permissions cannot be edited, so the merge step in CI needs a new token 7. Supabase plans a separate Merge permission later 7. The page went up on 16 November, four days after the change 7.

17 November: new Vercel teams pay for Standard builds by the minute. New Pro and Enterprise teams no longer include a Standard build slot 8. On Pro a Standard build costs US$0.014 per build minute, and the monthly usage credit applies 8. By that rate, 20 three-minute builds a day for 30 days is 1,800 minutes, US$25.20. The page speaks of new teams; it says nothing about teams created before 17 November 8.

20 November: Vercel Functions accept request bodies up to 20 MiB, in public beta. The limit was 4.5 MB 9. The opt-in is the environment variable VERCEL_SUPPORT_LARGE_REQUEST_BODY=1, per project and per environment, and it requires the performance memory setting of 4 GB 9. It covers the Node.js, Python and Bun runtimes; the Edge runtime stays at 4.5 MB and answers 413 to a larger body 9. With the opt-in on, Routing Middleware (code that runs before the function) receives headers and no body, so middleware that reads the body stops seeing it 9.

items.title: One Cloudflare Pages line moved a domain: 147 of 147 URLs in one hop, POSTs become GETs
items.summary: One _redirects line sends each old path and its query string to the new address. Left without a code, the line is a 302. A 301 drops a form's POST. A 16-line check, and what Google's Change of Address tool asks for.
items.content_html:
A site that changes its address needs each old URL to answer with a redirect to the same page at the new address. On Cloudflare Pages that is one line in a text file. This week we moved a 147-page site of ours from its own domain, defiant.to, to a folder on GitHub Pages. Measured today: 147 of 147 old URLs reach their new page in one hop. The same line turns a form's POST into a GET, and the line's default status code is the temporary one.

One line carries each path and its query string

Cloudflare Pages reads a file named _redirects in the published folder. Each line is a source, a destination and an optional status code 1. An asterisk in the source matches the rest of the path, and :splat in the destination puts it back 1:

/* https://example.github.io/newsite/:splat 301

A Pages project whose only file is this one, with the old domain attached as its custom domain, is the whole redirect server. Three facts from Cloudflare's page, read today 1:

  • The code is optional and defaults to 302, a temporary redirect. A line without 301 moves visitors and says the move is temporary.
  • A file takes 2,000 static lines and 100 lines with a splat or placeholder. A whole-domain move uses one of the 100.
  • Redirects in the file do not apply to requests that a Pages Function (server code inside the project) answers.

Cloudflare's pricing page says requests that invoke no Function are free and unlimited on the free and the paid plans 2. A project with one text file invokes none.

What the line does with awkward requests, measured 21 November 2026 with curl, one request each:

Request to the old domainAnswer
/about/301 to /newsite/about/
/about/?utm_source=x&id=7301, query string intact
/a%20b/%E0%B8%81/ (a space and a Thai letter, encoded)301, encoding intact
/no-such-page/301; the new host then answers 404
//about/301 to /newsite/about/, the double slash folded to one
HEAD /about/301
http:// in place of https://301 to https:// on the old domain first, then the line

The 301 carries no Cache-Control header. RFC 9110 lets a browser cache a 301 on its own judgement 5, so a wrong destination shipped for an hour can sit in visitors' browsers after the fix.

147 of 147 land in one hop; a missing slash costs a second hop

The new site's sitemap (its list of pages) has 147 URLs 3. We requested each one on the old domain and followed the redirects: 147 answered 200 at the matching new URL after one hop. Then the 146 URLs other than the home page, with the final slash removed, as people type them: 146 answered 200 after two hops, because GitHub Pages adds the slash with a 301 of its own.

Google's page on site moves advises a redirect straight to the final URL, says Googlebot follows up to 10 hops, and says to leave the redirects in place for at least a year 4.

A 301 turns a form's POST into a GET

A form or a webhook (a message one service posts to another) sends a POST: a request with data in its body. RFC 9110 says of the 301:

a user agent MAY change the request method from POST to GET

and names the 308 as the code that forbids the change 5. Measured today, a POST to a made-up path on the old domain:

ClientAfter the 301Final answer
curl, following redirectsGET, body dropped404
curl with --post301POST405 from GitHub Pages

GitHub Pages serves files and answers a POST with 405, so a 308 changes nothing when the new host is static. The form needs a receiver of its own and the page needs to post to it by full address. Our site's sign-up form posts to a Cloudflare Worker on a separate hostname; the redirect line plays no part in it. Before a move, the list to make is each place outside the site that posts to the old domain: payment webhooks, form services, apps.

Google's tool accepts a folder as the destination, and takes each hostname separately

Search Console's Change of Address tool tells Google that a site moved. Its help page, read today 6:

  • The old site is a domain or subdomain. A folder cannot be the starting point, and a folder on another domain can be the destination.
  • www does not move with the bare domain. Each hostname variant of the old site is filed on its own.
  • The tool checks for 301s on a few pages before it accepts the request.
  • Google forwards signals for 180 days. After that it treats the old site, if still up, as unrelated.
  • The page recommends paying for the old domain for at least a year, so that nobody else buys it.

What GitHub Pages allows

GitHub's limits page, read today: a published site of at most 1 GB, a soft limit of 100 GB of traffic a month, and a use policy against using it as free hosting for an online shop or a paid software service 7. A shop or a paid app goes on a different host; the redirect line is the same there.

The check, 16 lines

The script reads the new site's sitemap, requests each page at the old domain, and prints each URL that does not reach its new page with a 200 in one hop.

import re, subprocess, sys, urllib.request

new, old = sys.argv[1].rstrip("/"), sys.argv[2].rstrip("/")
xml = urllib.request.urlopen(new + "/sitemap.xml").read().decode()
locs = re.findall(r"<loc>([^<]+)", xml)
bad = 0
for loc in locs:
    out = subprocess.run(
        ["curl", "-s", "-o", "/dev/null", "-L", "-w",
         "%{num_redirects} %{http_code} %{url_effective}", old + loc[len(new):]],
        capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.split()
    if out != ["1", "200", loc]:
        bad += 1
        print("BAD", old + loc[len(new):], *out)
print(len(locs), "checked,", bad, "bad")
sys.exit(1 if bad else 0)
python3 move_check.py https://example.github.io/newsite https://old-domain.example

On our move it printed 147 checked, 0 bad in 43 seconds. It reads the new sitemap, so an old URL that has no page on the new site is outside it; the old site's own sitemap or server log, saved before the switch, covers those. Moving a site between hosts, each page checked, is a service we sell 8.

items.title: Order tickets from four open models: symbol codes silently wrong 186 times in 660, JSON 46
items.summary: An ITMO paper says a ticket's format changes how often a small model writes a valid, wrong order. Prompting four models on Workers AI, symbol codes did worst on all four and JSON best; a word check caught 28 of JSON's 46.
items.content_html:
Asked to turn "five small lattes please, all hot" into a ticket for the bar, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash wrote 1 small hot latte on one of two tries. The ticket has the right form, a program reading it finds no fault, and four lattes are missing. A paper from ITMO University, posted on 12 November 2026, calls this a silent error and reports that the format of the ticket changes how often it happens 1. On 20 November 2026 we ran a small version on four open models (models whose weights are published) on Cloudflare Workers AI. With the ticket in symbol codes, 186 of 660 tickets were valid and wrong. In JSON, 46 of 660.

In the paper, plain words beat JSON on models under a billion parameters

The authors fine-tuned (trained further, on examples of the task) two small models, Qwen3.5-0.8B and LFM2.5-350M, to write pizza orders in six formats that carry the same information. They scored 1,357 orders written by people 1. On Qwen, 4.5% of the tickets in plain words were silent errors, 8.3% in a symbol format of the same length, and 14.9% in JSON, the text format of braces and quoted names that most software reads. A words ticket took 10.9 output tokens against 44.1 for JSON 1. A token is the piece of text a model reads or writes: a word or part of one.

The paper's own limits: both models are under a billion parameters, and the effect may shrink with larger ones 1. A shop building an order bot today is more likely to send a prompt (written instructions and a few examples) to a larger hosted model. We measured that case.

A companion demo runs the fine-tuned 0.8B model inside a browser tab: type an order and read the ticket it writes 23. The code is on GitHub; the repository names no licence 4.

With a prompt, symbols did worst on all four models and JSON best

One order, "two large iced lattes with oat milk, no sugar", in our four formats:

FormatTicket
Words2 large iced latte with oat milk no sugar
Symbols2 latte L I oat_milk !sugar
JSON{"orders":[{"n":2,"drink":"latte","size":"large","temp":"iced","attrs":[{"thing":"oat milk"},{"thing":"sugar","not":true}]}]}
JSON, words insidethe same, with "attrs":["with oat milk","no sugar"]

In the symbol format ! means none, + extra and - less, as in the paper's 1. Each reply lands in one of the paper's four outcomes 1: right; silent (a program reads it as a ticket, and the order is wrong); broken (a program cannot read it); refused. Silent tickets, with broken ones in brackets:

ModelWordsSymbolsJSONJSON, words inside
Granite 4.0 H Micro, of 18038 (24)97 (7)36 (7)34 (3)
Llama 4 Scout, of 1803 (6)44 (1)0 (0)0 (0)
Mistral Small 3.1, of 18021 (0)29 (1)9 (0)12 (0)
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, of 12015 (0)16 (0)1 (0)5 (0)
All four, of 66077 (30)186 (9)46 (7)51 (3)

Mistral also refused one order three times in each JSON format. Llama 4 Scout, a 17-billion-parameter model 5, wrote 360 of 360 JSON tickets right.

The paper's first result repeated: words had fewer silent errors than symbols on all four models, by one ticket on DeepSeek. Its second did not: one of the two JSON formats had the fewest silent errors on all four.

We did not turn on JSON mode, the setting that forces a reply to be valid JSON. The paper's point about it: forcing the form removes broken tickets and leaves the silent ones 1.

Symbols got misread, lines lost counts, words broke in view

Symbols. Of the 170 silent symbol tickets from the three smaller models, 81 mixed up "has", "extra" and "less", and 74 had a wrong size or temperature. "a medium cappuccino with cinnamon on top" came back from Granite and from Llama 4 Scout as 1 cappuccino M +cinnamon, three times of three each: extra cinnamon.

Lines. 31 of the 77 silent words tickets had the wrong number of drinks, against 5 of JSON's 46. In JSON the count has a name, "n". On a line it is a bare number at the start.

Words. Granite wrote 3 iced thai tea with extra ice, the customer's phrase in place of the format's extra ice. 24 of its 180 words tickets did not parse (a program could not read them). A broken ticket is in view: the program asks again.

"No". The paper traces much of its gain to negation 1. Here, writing "none" as a flag ("not":true) or as a word ("no sugar") made no difference: the three smaller models made 4 negation errors in 540 tickets with the flag and 6 in 540 with the word, and DeepSeek made none.

A word check caught 28 of the 46 silent JSON tickets

A size or temperature on the ticket that the customer did not type, one the customer typed that the ticket lacks, or a drink or topping whose name is not in the message:

import re
SIZES_TEMPS = ["small", "medium", "large", "hot", "iced"]

def disagrees(message, orders):
    msg = message.lower()
    said = {w for w in SIZES_TEMPS if re.search(rf"\b{w}\b", msg)}
    on_ticket = set()
    for o in orders:
        on_ticket |= {o[k] for k in ("size", "temp") if o.get(k)}
        names = [o["drink"]] + [a["thing"] for a in o.get("attrs", [])]
        if any(n.split()[0] not in msg for n in names):
            return True
    return on_ticket != said

Run on the 650 JSON tickets that parsed, it flagged 28 of the 46 silent ones and 19 of the 604 right ones. The right ones it flags are corrections: "a large latte, wait, make that a medium" names two sizes. The check does not read counts: of the 5 JSON tickets with a wrong number of drinks it flagged 3, each for another fault.

For a shop that takes orders by chat

  1. Ask the model for JSON with named fields and plain-word values. Where the kitchen screen wants codes, map to them in code afterwards.
  2. Count the four outcomes on 50 of your own past messages before choosing a model. Here Granite cost US$0.009 per 1,000 tickets and got 36 of 180 silently wrong in JSON; Llama 4 Scout cost US$0.13 per 1,000 and got 0 of 180 wrong (prices read 20 November 2026 6).
  3. Run a word check like the one above and send a ticket that disagrees back to the customer as a question.
  4. Read the ticket back before the bar starts: "2 large iced lattes, oat milk, no sugar. Right?" A wrong count passes the format check and the word check; the customer sees it.

Hongdam builds automations in n8n, Make, Zapier or code 9.

Run it yourself

The JSON prompt, as the system message, with the customer's text as the user message:

You turn a customer's drink order into a ticket for the bar.

Menu
Drinks: latte, americano, cappuccino, mocha, thai tea, green tea, cocoa
Sizes: small, medium, large
Temperature: hot, iced
Things a drink can have, have none of, have extra of, or have less of:
sugar, ice, milk, oat milk, whipped cream, honey, cinnamon, shot

Write only what the customer asked for: no size or temperature the customer
did not say. Apply any correction the customer makes. Drinks that differ go
on separate lines of the ticket. If the message is not a drink order, reply
with {"reject":true}
Reply with the ticket only, no other text.

Ticket format
One JSON object on one line: {"orders":[...]}. Each order: "n" (count),
"drink", optional "size", optional "temp" ("hot" or "iced"), optional "attrs".
Each attr: {"thing":"<thing>"} (has it), {"thing":"<thing>","not":true}
(none of it), {"thing":"<thing>","qty":"extra"} or {"thing":"<thing>","qty":"less"}.

Examples

Customer: three americanos, one without milk
Ticket:
{"orders":[{"n":2,"drink":"americano"},{"n":1,"drink":"americano","attrs":[{"thing":"milk","not":true}]}]}

Our prompt had four examples; the other formats got the same four, rewritten.

How we measured

We wrote 60 orders: 20 plain, 25 with a negation or a decoy ("no rush, but could i get…"), 15 with a correction or a split ("four americanos, two with milk and two without"). The paper's benchmark, PIZZA, is under a non-commercial licence 1, so its orders are not in our test. Each right ticket is our reading of the order.

Models: @cf/ibm-granite/granite-4.0-h-micro, @cf/meta/llama-4-scout-17b-16e-instruct, @cf/mistralai/mistral-small-3.1-24b-instruct and @cf/deepseek-ai/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017, through Workers AI's chat endpoint on 20 November 2026, temperature (the randomness setting) left at the platform's value, 200 output tokens allowed. Each order ran three times per format on the first three models and twice on DeepSeek, 2,640 tickets in all. A call was about 420 input tokens and 20 output tokens. DeepSeek's limit is 20 requests a minute on standard billing 7; 26 of its first 240 calls came back HTTP 429 (too many requests) and were sent again.

Some replies ran on into an invented next customer. We cut each reply at the first line starting "Customer:", as a stop sequence (a string that ends the reply) would, and removed code fences. Each parser accepts what its prompt describes. Two tickets match when they list the same drinks in any order; 2 latte equals two lines of 1 latte.

Not measured: output tokens per format. In characters, the right tickets average 31 in words, 23 in symbols, 101 in JSON and 85 in JSON with words inside.

Left out of the tables: three older Llama models. Llama 3.2 1B and 3B are listed for retirement on 20 November 2026 8, and we found no model page for Llama 3.1 8B fast. On the 3B and the 8B, symbols were again the worst format. On the 3B, words had fewer silent tickets than JSON, 59 against 86 of 180, the paper's direction. The 1B wrote broken tickets at least 152 times of 180 in each format.

items.title: n8n 2.48.4 and 2.47.7 stop blanking the execution page for a global credential
items.summary: An execution that used a global credential came back as 'Data redacted' with no reveal button, even for the user who ran it. Fixed in 2.48.4 and 2.47.7 on 13 November, 2.49.0 on 17 November.
items.content_html:
n8n 2.48.4 and 2.47.7 shipped a single bug fix on 13 November 2026: "Stop redacting executions that use global credentials" 12. The same change landed on master on 10 November 3; the 2.49.0 pre-release carried it forward on 17 November 8. One block removed in one file does the work 7.

A redacted run that you cannot un-redact

n8n has an execution-data redaction feature. The docs set two triggers: a per-workflow toggle ("Redact production execution data" and "Redact manual execution data") and an instance-level policy a license can enforce 6. When redaction fires, the execution page shows node names, status and timing, and replaces each payload with a "Data redacted" indicator and a shredder icon. A user with execution:reveal — instance owners, admins and project admins by default — can press Reveal data, confirm an audit warning, and read the payload for that session 6.

There is a second redaction path the docs do not describe: the credential check. When you view an execution, n8n also asks whether you can use every credential the workflow referenced. If you cannot, the payload is blanked and the reveal button is hidden. The PR puts the case plainly 3:

Redaction hides execution data from a viewer who cannot use a credential that the workflow references.

That check ignored the instance-wide credential:use scope of owners and admins, and it left out global credentials — the kind every user on the installation may use. An execution that touched a global credential came back blanked for every viewer, with no reveal button to recover it.

The shape of the blank

The PR's integration test seeds a project with a credential marked isGlobal: true, runs a workflow that reads it, and views the execution as a plain member 3. Before the fix: redactionInfo was {reason: 'credential_inaccessible', canReveal: false} — no payload, no reveal button. After: redactionInfo is undefined, and the JSON output appears as it did on the run itself. A second test covers the opposite case, a non-global credential the member cannot use: redacted as before, reveal still denied.

The changed file is packages/@n8n/backend-services/src/credentials/credentials-finder.service.ts 7. The function at the centre is findCredentialIdsWithScopeForUser, called by three paths that answer "as if this user had no instance-wide credential:use": the redaction check, a team-project run check, and a publish check. The diff removes the enclosing if (!options.ignoreGlobalOverride) so the global-credentials lookup runs regardless of that option.

-        // Also include global credentials if scopes allow read-only access.
-        if (!options.ignoreGlobalOverride) {
-            if (this.hasGlobalReadOnlyAccess(scopes)) {
-                const globalIds = await this.credentialAccessRepository.findGlobalProjectCredentialIds(
-                    credentialIds,
-                    false,
-                );
-                for (const id of globalIds) result.add(id);
-            } else if (this.hasGlobalConnectAccess(scopes)) {
-                // ...connect access branch...
-            }
-        }
+        // Also include global credentials if scopes allow read-only access. Every user
+        // may use a global credential, so this applies even when the instance-wide
+        // override is ignored.
+        if (this.hasGlobalReadOnlyAccess(scopes)) {
+            const globalIds = await this.credentialAccessRepository.findGlobalProjectCredentialIds(
+                credentialIds,
+                false,
+            );
+            for (const id of globalIds) result.add(id);
+        } else if (this.hasGlobalConnectAccess(scopes)) {
+            // ...connect access branch...
+        }

Measured 19 November 2026 from GitHub's /pulls/43223/files endpoint: +18 and -17 lines in the finder, +27 and -1 in its unit test, +131 and -0 in a new integration test. One block removed; ignoreGlobalOverride no longer suppresses the global-credentials lookup.

Which versions carry it

Release lineVersionDatePR
masterthe merge on 10 Nov 202610 Nov#43223 3
2.48.x2.48.413 Nov#43775 4
2.47.x2.47.713 Nov#43776 5
2.49.x pre-release2.49.017 Nov8

2.48.5 (18 November) and the 2.49.1 beta (18 November) include the same fix with later patches on top 8.

What a viewer sees after upgrading

An execution whose workflow used a global credential, viewed under the upgraded installation, shows its node payloads with no "Data redacted" indicator for viewers with read access to the workflow. An execution that used a credential the viewer cannot use is redacted as before, with the reveal button for admins. The fix narrows what the credential check covers; the per-workflow redaction toggles, the instance policy and the reveal audit trail do not change 6.

For a team running n8n in Docker, the upgrade path is docker pull n8nio/n8n:2.48.4 (or :2.47.7) and a container restart. GET /rest/settings returns the running version in versionCli.

items.title: OpenSSH 10.6p2 shut the 300-byte password bypass on Alpine sshd: fixed in every branch
items.summary: A password 256 to 1024 bytes long logged into Alpine accounts whose shadow field was *, because musl's crypt() returned the single character * on overflow. OpenSSH 10.6p2, released 5 November, blocks it.
items.content_html:
OpenSSH 10.6p2 shipped on 5 November 2026 with one change marked security: "avoid password authentication bypass that is exploitable through sshd(8) that affects some Linux systems when built and run with PAM support disabled" 2. PAM, Pluggable Authentication Modules, is the chain of authentication steps most Linux distributions put between sshd and the password file; a build without PAM compares the submitted password to the shadow entry directly. The GitHub Security Advisory names the condition precisely: "sshd in OpenSSH before 10.6p2 on Linux, when musl libc is used without PAM, lacks a workaround for a password authentication bypass" 3. musl is the small C library Alpine Linux ships; the default Alpine sshd build uses musl and no PAM. On 9 November CISA added CVE-2026-123158 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog with a 12 November deadline 1. The CVSS score is 8.1 (High), vector AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H 3.

For some accounts, any password between 256 and 1024 characters succeeded 3. The "some" matters: musl's crypt() returns the string * on overflow, and when the shadow entry is also *, OpenSSH compared * to * and accepted the login.

The patch requires the stored hash to be at least four characters

The OpenSSH portable commit 4353fdc adds #define MIN_PASSWORD_HASH_LEN 4 and refuses to compare a candidate against a stored hash shorter than that 4. A full crypt() hash is dozens of characters — a modern yescrypt or SHA-512 entry starts with $y$ or $6$ and runs to about eighty. A shadow field of *, ! or !! is one or two characters and signals a locked account: no password login allowed. The old code treated the one-character * returned by musl's failing crypt() as if it were a hash, matched it against the one-character * in shadow, and let the attacker in. The new code refuses the comparison. The same commit also replaces raw pw->pw_passwd pointers with xstrdup copies and frees them in pick_salt, so the fallback path for unknown users owns its own memory 4. The release notes say the root cause lies outside sshd but sshd can avoid it 2: the underlying bug is musl returning * for an oversized input, and the OpenSSH change is the workaround.

Which Alpine containers have sshd and no PAM by default

A base alpine:* image has neither openssh-server nor PAM. The ones to look at are:

  • the official Alpine cloud images and ISOs, which run sshd during install and on first boot
  • the linuxserver.io/openssh-server image and hobby-server images derived from it
  • a Dockerfile that installs openssh-server on top of alpine:* (and no PAM)
  • devcontainer and CI base images built the same way
  • Alpine on OpenWrt, Buildroot, Yocto and embedded gadgets with sshd enabled 3

apk info openssh-server prints the installed version. The default Alpine package does not pull PAM in. A rule of thumb on a fresh install: if apk info -q openssh-server-pam prints nothing, PAM is off and the bypass path applies.

Every supported Alpine branch has the fix in its repository

Measured 18 November 2026, 06:35 Bangkok time. APKINDEX.tar.gz was pulled from dl-cdn.alpinelinux.org for each branch and the openssh-server version read out. The secdb entry for each branch was then checked against the CVE-2026-123158 row 5.

Only edge ships OpenSSH 10.6p2 itself; stable branches carry the fix as a backport on the version of OpenSSH they already shipped, so ssh -V still prints the older number after apk upgrade. The secdb file for each branch names the fixed version against CVE-2026-123158 5; the current package in the branch's index on dl-cdn.alpinelinux.org matches that number 6.

Two commands show where an Alpine host stands

# Installed version — compare against the table above.
apk info -v openssh-server 2>/dev/null
# PAM state. Empty output means PAM is not installed, so the bypass path applied before the patch.
apk info -q openssh-server-pam 2>/dev/null
# Accounts whose shadow field was the attacker's target.
# These are locked system accounts: login was never meant to work on them.
awk -F: '$2=="*" || $2=="!" || $2=="!!" {print $1}' /etc/shadow

To apply the fix: apk update && apk upgrade openssh-server && rc-service sshd restart. sshd must restart; running sshd processes run the old code until they do. A container image rebuild pulls the patched package on the next apk add openssh-server from a branch whose index now points at the fixed version 6.

Three settings make the bypass path unreachable without an upgrade. PasswordAuthentication no in /etc/ssh/sshd_config switches sshd to public keys only; a keyless home-lab host is the usual case for yes. Installing openssh-server-pam switches the authentication chain to PAM, which goes through glibc-style password handling even on musl. UsePAM yes then takes effect. Any one of the three closes the path the GHSA describes 3; combined with the upgrade, they are belts around a belt.

The research named it SSHole; CISA names it CVE-2026-123158

A password openssl rand -base64 384 | tr -d '\n' is 512 characters. On an unpatched Alpine sshd with a locked root account whose shadow field is *, that password logged in as root. The CWE is 394, Unexpected Status Code or Return Value 3 — the status code musl's crypt() returned (*) was mistaken for a hash.

Red Hat's advisory records the mechanism in one sentence: on Linux with musl and no PAM, "the SSH server can misinterpret input strings as password hashes" 7. Red Hat Enterprise Linux and Fedora use glibc and ship PAM, so they are not affected 7. The same is true of Debian, Ubuntu, Arch and openSUSE out of the box. The exposed hosts are the ones the GHSA names: Alpine, and musl builds on OpenWrt, Buildroot and Yocto 3.

items.title: Supabase turned off four TLS 1.2 ciphers: 9 of 163 recorded clients now fail to connect
items.summary: The removal announced for 10 November is in effect on project APIs. Safari 5 to 8, Chrome 30 and Opera 17 fail at the handshake; IE 11 connects through the ECDSA certificate. Measured 17 November 2026.
items.content_html:
Supabase's changelog and docs, read 17 November 2026, still speak in the future tense: four TLS 1.2 cipher suites leave project APIs "on November 10, 2026, at the earliest" 12. The removal is in effect. TLS is the encryption under HTTPS, and a cipher suite is one of the methods a client and a server can agree on for it. On 17 November all four suites fail on <project_ref>.supabase.co and still connect on api.supabase.com, the Management API, which the change leaves out 1.

A client that fails does so in the handshake, the exchange that opens the connection, before it sends a request. The request does not appear in the project's API logs 3.

The four suites fail on project hosts and still connect on the Management API

OpenSSL 3.6.4, s_client, TLS 1.2, one suite offered at a time, against three project hosts named in Supabase's public repositories and against api.supabase.com. Measured 17 November 2026, 06:42 Bangkok time. The three project hosts answered alike.

OfferedProject hostapi.supabase.com
ECDHE-ECDSA-AES128-SHA256handshake failureconnects
ECDHE-RSA-AES128-SHA256handshake failureconnects
ECDHE-ECDSA-AES256-SHA384handshake failureconnects
ECDHE-RSA-AES256-SHA384handshake failureconnects
the six GCM and ChaCha20 suites Supabase lists as staying 2connects, each oneconnects, each one
TLS 1.3connectsconnects
TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1protocol version alertprotocol version alert

9 of 163 recorded clients are cut off: Safari 5 to 8, Chrome 30, Opera 17

SSL Labs publishes the ClientHello of 163 clients it recorded, from Android 2.3.7 to Chrome 131 4. The ClientHello is the first message a client sends: the TLS versions and cipher suites it can use. Its API at api.ssllabs.com/api/v3/getClients returns the bytes. A script put a project's host name and a fresh random value into each one, sent it, and read the reply: a ServerHello naming the chosen suite, or an alert. Each client went once to three project hosts and once to api.supabase.com. The three project hosts gave the same 163 answers.

Result on a project hostClientsWhich
Connect, TLS 1.318
Connect, TLS 1.29190 on ECDHE-ECDSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256; Chrome 49 on XP SP3 on the RSA form
Fail; connect on the Management API9Safari 5 on iOS 5.1.1, 6 on iOS 6.0.1, 7 on iOS 7.1 and OS X 10.9, 8 on iOS 8.0 beta, iOS 8.4 and OS X 10.10; Chrome 30 and Opera 17 on Windows 7
Refused on both, protocol version36clients that stop at TLS 1.0 or 1.1
Refused on both, handshake failure9Android 2.3.7, IE 6 and IE 8 on XP, Java 6u45, three crawlers from 2013 and 2014

On the Management API all nine chose ECDHE-ECDSA-AES128-SHA256, one of the four removed. The oldest recorded versions that connect to a project: Safari 9 (iOS 9, OS X 10.11), Chrome 31, Firefox 27, Android 4.4.2, IE 11 on Windows 7, Java 8, OpenSSL 1.0.1h.

Two limits. The replay reads the server's answer to the first message and does not finish the handshake. And the recorded list is browsers, a few runtimes and crawlers; it has no smart TV or set-top box, the devices Supabase names first 2.

IE 11 on Windows 7 and 8.1 connects because one certificate is ECDSA

A certificate proves the server's identity, and its key is one of two kinds, RSA or ECDSA. A project host presents either: OpenSSL received a 2048-bit RSA certificate when it offered an RSA suite and a 256-bit ECDSA one when it offered an ECDSA suite. Twelve recorded IE 11 clients, on Windows 7, Windows 8.1 and Windows Phone 8.1, list no GCM or ChaCha20 suite for RSA. They connect on ECDHE-ECDSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256. With an RSA certificate alone they would have failed with the nine.

A custom domain was not measured. Whether it presents an ECDSA certificate decides those twelve.

Java 7 with TLS 1.2 switched on is cut off too

By default Java 7 enables TLS 1.0 alone for clients, and its cipher list has no GCM suite; the SHA256 and SHA384 suites on it are CBC ones 5. The recorded Java 7u25 hello stops at TLS 1.0 and was refused before the change. An OpenSSL hello restricted to TLS 1.2 and 16 CBC suites from Java 7's list failed on the project host and connected on the Management API. A server integration written on Java 7 and set to TLS 1.2 by hand is that client. Java reports SSLHandshakeException: Received fatal alert: handshake_failure 3.

A web app built with Vite's defaults targets browsers far newer than the nine

Vite's default build target is Chrome 111, Edge 111, Firefox 114, Safari 16.4 and iOS 16.4 7. Safari 8 and Chrome 30 sit far below that target, so a site built that way is unlikely to have worked in the nine before this week. The clients to look for are the ones that call the project without loading the site: older releases of a mobile or desktop app, devices, and scripts or servers on old runtimes 2.

Two commands show where a project or custom domain stands

HOST=<project_ref>.supabase.co   # or the custom domain
openssl s_client -connect $HOST:443 -servername $HOST -tls1_2 \
  -cipher ECDHE-RSA-AES128-SHA256 </dev/null 2>&1 | grep -E "Cipher is|alert"
openssl s_client -connect $HOST:443 -servername $HOST -tls1_2 \
  -cipher ECDHE-ECDSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256 </dev/null 2>&1 | grep -E "Cipher is|alert"

After the removal the first prints alert handshake failure. The second prints the suite when an ECDSA certificate is there. To test a client, run curl -v https://$HOST/rest/v1/ on the old machine: HTTP 401 with "No API key found in request" means TLS worked; curl exit code 35 means the handshake failed.

A proxy on workers.dev lets the nine back in, and 30 TLS 1.0 and 1.1 clients with them

For a client that cannot be updated, Supabase's guide names a proxy under your control that accepts the old suites and forwards to the project 3. Cloudflare's edge lists CBC suites among those it supports by default 6. The same 163 hellos against a workers.dev host: 147 connect, 18 on TLS 1.3, 99 on TLS 1.2, 5 on TLS 1.1 and 25 on TLS 1.0. The nine all connect, on ECDHE-ECDSA-AES128-SHA, a CBC suite with SHA-1 that is older than the four Supabase removed.

export default {
  async fetch(request, env) {
    const url = new URL(request.url);
    url.protocol = "https:";
    url.hostname = env.SUPABASE_HOST; // <project_ref>.supabase.co
    url.port = "";
    return fetch(new Request(url, request));
  },
};

Run under wrangler dev (wrangler 4.163.0) on 17 November, this Worker returned the same 401 and body for /rest/v1/ as the project did directly. It was not deployed, and Realtime's WebSocket and Auth redirects were not tested. Pointing the old clients alone at the proxy leaves every other client on the direct route and the stronger suites.
