items.title: Inkling 2 Small on Workers AI: reasoning_effort none still thinks, and bills for it
items.summary: Cloudflare added Thinking Machines' open model on 12 November. In 300 graded calls today, none still reasoned in 30 of 30 replies and used 16% more tokens than the default. minimal was the cheapest setting with every task right.
items.content_html:
Cloudflare put Inkling 2 Small, the open-weights model from Thinking Machines Lab, on Workers AI on 12 November 2026 1. Its page lists six reasoning levels, and the changelog says to set reasoning_effort "to none to turn reasoning off" 12. On 16 November 2026 we sent ten builder tasks, three runs each, at every level through Workers AI's OpenAI-compatible endpoint. At none, all 30 replies came back with reasoning, and the 30 runs billed 21,370 output tokens: 16% more than the default high, 76% more than minimal.

Reasoning is the working a model writes before its answer. Workers AI returns it in a separate reasoning_content field and bills it as output. A token is the unit a model reads and writes, about three quarters of an English word.

US$0.30 in, US$1.00 out, on the paid plan only

Thinking Machines announced the model on 5 November and released the weights on 12 November under the Apache 2.0 licence 57. It is a mixture-of-experts model, one that uses a small part of itself for each token: 594 billion parameters, 17 billion active 57 (Cloudflare's page says 18 2). The context window on Workers AI is 1,048,576 tokens 2.

Prices read 16 November 2026: US$0.30 per million input tokens, US$1.00 per million output, US$0.10 for cached input 3. That is twice GLM-5.3 Flash (US$0.15 and US$0.50 3), which Workers AI stops serving on 20 November 8. Inkling 2 Small needs the Workers Paid plan or prepaid AI Gateway credits, so the free 10,000 neurons a day do not cover it 23. A neuron is Workers AI's billing unit; 1,000 cost US$0.011 3. The rate limit is 20 requests a minute on standard billing and 50 with prepaid credits 4. We sent 18 a minute for twelve minutes and no call was refused.

Five levels change the bill; none lands near the default

reasoning_effortCorrect of 30Replies with reasoningOutput tokensSeconds, medianNeuronsUS$ at list price
none303021,3701.42,0300.0223
minimal303012,1711.11,1940.0131
low293014,5801.11,4130.0155
medium303018,3731.31,7580.0193
high (default)303018,4011.31,7610.0194
max303023,8271.42,2540.0248

minimal wrote fewer tokens than high on all ten tasks, by median, and low on eight. medium and high came out 28 tokens apart over 30 runs. none sat between high and max.

The model's chat template, the file that turns a request into the text the model reads, maps the six names to numbers: none 0, minimal 0.1, low 0.2, medium 0.7, high 0.9, max 0.99. It writes the number into a system line that starts "Thinking effort level:" 6. Our 30 prompts counted 3,216 input tokens at none, the same as at each of the other five names, and 3,156 with thinking switched off the other way (next section): 2 fewer per prompt. That fits none reaching the model as a number other than 0. Workers AI does not return the rendered prompt, so the cause is unknown. It does check the field: "NONE", "0", a bare number 0 and an invented word each returned HTTP 400.

enable_thinking: false switches it off, and the arithmetic goes with it

Sending {"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false}} in place of reasoning_effort did what none did not. 28 of 30 replies carried no reasoning, and the 30 runs billed 2,785 output tokens, 85% fewer than high, for 339 neurons.

19 of 30 were correct. The crontab line, the SQL, the Thai order turned into JSON, both Python tasks and the date count passed three times of three. The VAT total failed twice, and the bill, the calendar count and the puzzle failed every time. In two puzzle replies the model wrote its working into the answer in front of the right JSON, so an app parsing the reply as JSON gets an error.

For an app on Inkling 2 Small today:

  • Extraction, formatting, short code: enable_thinking false, about a fifth of the default bill.
  • Anything with numbers or conditions: minimal. It got 30 of 30 with 34% fewer tokens than the default.
  • none: read reasoning_content and usage.completion_tokens in one of your own replies before counting on it.
import json, os, urllib.request

ACCOUNT, TOKEN = os.environ["CF_ACCOUNT_ID"], os.environ["CF_API_TOKEN"]
URL = f"https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/{ACCOUNT}/ai/v1/chat/completions"

def ask(prompt, **setting):
    body = dict({"model": "@cf/thinkingmachines/inkling-2-small", "max_tokens": 8192,
                 "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]}, **setting)
    req = urllib.request.Request(URL, json.dumps(body).encode(),
                                 {"Authorization": f"Bearer {TOKEN}", "Content-Type": "application/json"})
    reply = json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=600))
    msg, usage = reply["choices"][0]["message"], reply["usage"]
    return msg["content"], len(msg.get("reasoning_content") or ""), usage["completion_tokens"]

q = "37 mugs at 185 baht and 12 at 240 baht, 7% off the total. Baht to pay? Number only."
print(ask(q, reasoning_effort="none"))                           # reasoning length above 0 in our runs
print(ask(q, reasoning_effort="minimal"))
print(ask(q, chat_template_kwargs={"enable_thinking": False}))   # reasoning length 0

Against GLM-5.3 Flash and Gemma 4 26B, the same hour

30 runsCorrectOutput tokensSeconds, totalSeconds, medianNeurons

GLM-5.3 Flash, low279,5191661.7474
GLM-5.3 Flash, max2927,0272484.51,270
Gemma 4 26B, nothing set2855,1531,02418.71,533

Inkling's 30 runs took 36 to 60 seconds of call time at each level. Counting the Friday the 13ths from 2027 to 2030 (six) separated the models: Inkling got it 18 times of 18 across the six levels, Flash at low twice of three, and Gemma once, with two replies that ran to the 8,192-token allowance and returned nothing. Three Flash replies at low carried their thinking in the answer text.

Thai text takes 1.57 times the tokens of English

We counted input tokens for eight short shop texts in English and Thai, the method of our 30 October note with new texts 9.

ModelEnglishThaiThai ÷ EnglishInput price × multiple, US$ per million
Gemma 4 26B2913481.200.12
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 10172823971.410.42
GLM-5.3 Flash2858162.860.43
Inkling 2 Small3104861.570.47

List input prices read 16 November 2026 3. For Thai input, Inkling costs about what DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM-5.3 Flash do.

How we measured

Ten tasks a builder hands a model: an invoice with a service charge and VAT, days between two dates, Friday the 13ths in four years, a crontab line (the schedule format servers use) for a Bangkok time on a UTC server, an SQL query (a question to a database) run against a test table, a Thai LINE order turned into JSON (data in labelled fields), a Thai national ID check in Python run against test cases, a bug fixed in a median function, a three-server logic puzzle with one solution, and a 30-day token bill. A script graded each reply: the first number compared, SQL executed, JSON parsed, Python run. Each task ran three times at ten settings, 300 calls, through the chat completions endpoint between 13:35 and 13:47 Bangkok time on 16 November 2026, with a reply allowance of 8,192 tokens and temperature left at the platform's setting. No call failed. Token and neuron counts come from the replies; the 300 calls cost US$0.15 at list prices. The Thai count used 68 more calls with a one-line instruction in front, subtracted afterwards. We did not test the Workers binding (env.AI.run()), images, tools or long contexts. Hongdam picks the model and its settings for an assistant by running the customer's own tasks this way 10.

items.title: The week: a Workers spending limit, Node.js fixes 16 flaws, GitHub's brownout on Monday
items.summary: Four notes: GLM-5.3 Flash's replacements measured, Supabase CLI v3 in CI, llama.cpp 1.0.0, checking AI crawlers. Plus five outside items, from a Workers spending limit to Copilot models ending 14 December.
items.content_html:
Since 13 November a Cloudflare account can put a spending limit on Workers and Durable Objects, and when the limit is reached Cloudflare blocks new Worker invocations until the next billing period or a higher limit 1. A Worker is a small program that runs on Cloudflare's servers each time a request arrives; a loop, a bot or a viral day can run up its bill overnight. That leads the five outside items. First, the week's four notes.

Four notes, 9 to 14 November

Monday, models. GLM-5.3 Flash's replacements: Gemma 4 26B costs less per task, Qwen3.8 27B 3.6 times more: Workers AI stops serving GLM-5.3 Flash on 20 November, five days from today, and names two small models to move to. We ran ten builder tasks twice on each, 180 calls. With thinking on (the hidden reasoning a model writes before it answers) all four models got 20 of 20; Gemma 4 26B used 410 neurons, Cloudflare's billing unit, against 531 for Flash and 1,920 for Qwen3.8 27B. With thinking off the output tokens fell by 91 to 96% and the multi-step arithmetic failed. Both replacements run on the free daily allowance, which GLM-5.3 Flash does not.

Tuesday, last-mile. Supabase CLI v3 is the default since 2 November: a CI db push now stops for a yes: a deploy script that installs latest got v3 overnight. Database commands now target the copy of Supabase on the same computer unless given --remote, and a change to the hosted project fails where nobody can type yes, unless --yes is passed. We ran the same push on v2 and v3 the way a CI runner sees it. GitHub's code search found 4,728 public workflow files running supabase db push and 189 passing --yes. The note has both fixes: the v3 flags, or a pin to v2.

Friday, models. llama.cpp 1.0.0: 36 deprecated calls removed, --defrag-thold gone, FP8 KV cache on CUDA: the first major version of the program that runs open models on your own computer. Code using the 36 old function names stops compiling, and one grep in the note finds them. The KV cache (the model's memory of the conversation so far) can now be stored at 8 bits a value on NVIDIA cards, half of the default. The server refuses more by default: tools on a public address need an API key or a flag. Homebrew still gave 0.9.0 on release day.

Saturday, security. 16 of 31 AI crawler names publish an address list, one signs; reverse DNS names 3 of 12: a user agent, the name a visitor gives itself, is a claim anyone can type. We read the operator page behind each AI crawler name our traffic dashboard knows. Sixteen names have a published list of the addresses they crawl from, Exa signs its requests, six give a name and nothing to check it against. The older reverse DNS check named the operator for 3 lists of 12, because the AI companies crawl from rented cloud addresses. A 37-line checker in the note matches an address against the lists in under a millisecond.

Five items, 10 November to 14 December

Now: a spending limit for Workers and Durable Objects. In the dashboard, Billing, then Spend limits: a limit, an email and alert thresholds for each product, across the account for the current billing period 1. Turning off Block usage sends the email alerts and lets the app run on 1. The cf command-line tool sets the same thing, cf billing spend-policies create --product-id workers --threshold-cents 5000 --action usage_block for US$50 1. Cloudflare's page says reporting and blocking take time, so recorded spend can pass the limit, and it names no error code for a blocked request 1. AI Gateway's spend limits are a separate setting for Workers AI and other model bills 1. A prototype with a public URL and a card on file is the case for setting one today.

10 and 11 November: Node.js fixed 16 vulnerabilities. The releases are 26.13.1, 24.22.3 and 22.23.5 2; the release index dates the first two 10 November and 22.23.5 11 November 3. Seven of the 16 are rated high, most of them in HTTP/2 and TLS (the encryption under HTTPS), among them a use-after-free in respondWithFile() and a TLS 1.2 renegotiation that changes the server name and gets past client certificate checks 2. The high-rated ones are in Node's own HTTP/2 and TLS code, which a server runs when it handles those connections itself rather than behind a proxy. The index also lists 26.x as long-term support, code name Lithium 3. A Dockerfile pinned to node:24.22.2 or earlier needs the new number.

Monday 16 November, 16:00 to 18:00 UTC: GitHub's second pull_request_target brownout. pull_request_target runs a workflow with the base repository's secrets on a pull request from a fork 4. For those two hours, 23:00 to 01:00 in Thailand, public repositories on Free, Team and Enterprise Cloud see the runs that the 2 December default would block fail with an error annotation 4. Outside the window the rule runs in evaluate mode, with warnings 4. A failed run tomorrow night is the list of workflows to fix or to allow by name before 2 December.

8 December: Dependabot alerts pause on repositories with no activity in a year. Dependabot is GitHub's service that warns when a dependency has a known flaw. From 8 December it turns alerts off on repositories with no push, creation or alert switch-on in the past year, on every github.com plan 5. The alerts are archived, not deleted; any push turns them back on and restarts the year 5. Repositories under an enforced security configuration that turns alerts on are exempt 5. The page does not say whether Dependabot's security updates, the pull requests that fix the flaw, pause too 5. An old client site that still serves traffic from an untouched repository loses its warnings that day.

14 December: six models leave GitHub Copilot. Claude Fable 5, Claude Haiku 4.5, Gemini 3.8 Flash, Gemini 4 Argon, Grok 4.6 and Kimi K3 go from every Copilot experience; the suggested replacements are Fable 5.2, Haiku 5.5, Gemini 4 Hydrogen, Gemini 4 Carbon and Grok 4.7, with Kimi K3's to be announced 6. Haiku 4.5 stays for individual subscribers on annual plans 6. On Business and Enterprise the replacements switch on by themselves unless an administrator turned the default off 6. The page does not say what happens to a request that still names an old model after the date 6, so an integration or an agent setting that names one is the thing to change before it.

items.title: 16 of 31 AI crawler names publish an address list, one signs; reverse DNS names 3 of 12
items.summary: A user agent is a claim. Behind the 31 AI crawler names our traffic dashboard knows: 16 have a published address list, Exa signs, 6 give a name only. Reverse DNS fails on the AI companies' addresses. A 37-line checker.
items.content_html:
Every request to a website carries a user agent, a line of text in which the program asking names itself. Our traffic dashboard, traffic-eye, sorts visitors by that line; its classifier knows 31 AI crawler names, from ClaudeBot to MistralAI-User 1. Its README says what that is: a claim, since anyone can type Googlebot into the line 24. Today we read the operator page behind each of the 31 names to see which claims can be checked, and measured the two ways of checking.

16 names have a published address list, one has a signature, six have a name only

An address list is a file the operator publishes with the network ranges its crawler sends from, each range a prefix (a block of addresses written as a start and a size). Google publishes one for Googlebot. Read today, 14 November 2026, the AI operators have followed:

That is 16 names an address list covers, one that signs, six with a user agent and nothing to check it against. The eight remaining names (Bytespider, Diffbot, YouBot, Timpibot, Omgilibot, ImagesiftBot, Kangaroo Bot, Webzio) have no operator page we read today; their status is unknown.

Two things in the table are worth a second look. Bing's list carries a creation date of 3 January 2024, read from the file itself 5; it is the oldest. And DuckDuckGo's DuckAssistBot list is byte-for-byte the DuckDuckBot list, 486 addresses, same date; the two bots share addresses.

Reverse DNS names the operator for 3 lists of 12

The older check, the one Google documents, is reverse DNS: ask the address for its name, confirm the name ends in the operator's domain, then ask the name for its address and confirm it matches 4. We ran that on three addresses from each of 12 lists, the first host of the first, middle and last prefix, measured today from Chiang Rai:

ListName the address gives backOperator named
Googlebotcrawl-…googlebot.com, all three 4yes
bingbotmsnbot-…search.msn.com, all threeyes
CCBot…crawl.commoncrawl.org, all three 9yes
Applebot…applebot.apple.com for one of three, none for two 6partly
DuckDuckBot…crawl.duckduckgo.com for one of three, none for twopartly
AnthropicGoogle Cloud's generic …googleusercontent.com for two, none for oneno
PerplexityBot, Perplexity-UserAmazon's generic ec2-…amazonaws.com, all threeno
Amazonbotthe same Amazon namesno
GPTBot, ChatGPT-User, OAI-SearchBotno name at all, nine of nineno

The AI companies crawl from rented cloud addresses, and the cloud's reverse DNS names the cloud, not the tenant. A name under amazonaws.com says Amazon rents the address to someone; it does not say who. For ClaudeBot, GPTBot and PerplexityBot, the published list is the only check there is. Reflection's page says its addresses resolve under reflection.ai 12; its two prefixes were not in our sample.

The list check costs under a millisecond, the DNS check 47

The classifier's own comment explains why it stops at the user agent: reverse DNS "costs a lookup on every request" 1. The list check does not. The 15 lists the checker below reads are 1,714 prefixes and 105 kilobytes together, fetched once a day and loaded into memory; the match is arithmetic. For a Cloudflare Worker that means one scheduled fetch into KV (Cloudflare's key-value store) and a lookup per request that costs no network call.

This is the checker, 37 lines, tested today against Googlebot's and Anthropic's lists. Amazonbot is missing from it: Amazon's list is embedded in a web page, with no file address to fetch 10.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Is this request from the crawler it claims to be?  crawler_check.py <ip> "<user-agent>" """
import ipaddress, json, re, sys, urllib.request

LISTS = {  # user-agent token -> the operator's published address list
    r"ClaudeBot|Claude-User|Claude-SearchBot": "https://claude.com/crawling/bots.json",
    r"GPTBot": "https://openai.com/gptbot.json",
    r"ChatGPT-User": "https://openai.com/chatgpt-user.json",
    r"OAI-SearchBot": "https://openai.com/searchbot.json",
    r"Googlebot|Google-Extended": "https://developers.google.com/static/crawling/ipranges/common-crawlers.json",
    r"bingbot": "https://www.bing.com/toolbox/bingbot.json",
    r"Applebot": "https://search.developer.apple.com/applebot.json",
    r"PerplexityBot": "https://www.perplexity.com/perplexitybot.json",
    r"Perplexity-User": "https://www.perplexity.com/perplexity-user.json",
    r"DuckDuckBot": "https://duckduckgo.com/duckduckbot.json",
    r"DuckAssistBot": "https://duckduckgo.com/duckassistbot.json",
    r"CCBot": "https://index.commoncrawl.org/ccbot.json",
    r"MistralAI-User": "https://mistral.ai/mistralai-user-ips.json",
    r"Reflectionbot": "https://reflection.ai/bot/ips.json",
    r"KeenableBot": "https://app.keenable.ai/bot/keenablebot.json",
}

def prefixes(url):
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": "crawler-check/1.0"})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=20) as r:
        data = json.load(r)
    return [ipaddress.ip_network(p.get("ipv4Prefix") or p.get("ipv6Prefix"), strict=False) for p in data["prefixes"]]

def check(ip, ua):
    ip = ipaddress.ip_address(ip)
    for pat, url in LISTS.items():
        m = re.search(pat, ua, re.I)
        if m:
            hit = any(ip in n for n in prefixes(url))
            return "verified" if hit else "claims %s, address not on its list" % m.group(0)
    return "no published list for this user agent"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(check(sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]))

A request that says Googlebot from an address outside Google's list is the case the check exists for: on a shop's logs that is a scraper wearing a costume, and the costume is the reason it gets past a robots.txt that blocks scrapers by name. A request that says meta-externalagent cannot be checked this way at all; Meta's page offers no list 15.

The signature route: two key directories answer today, the draft that defines them has expired

Web Bot Auth is the newer idea: the crawler signs each request with a private key and names, in a Signature-Agent header, the site where its public key is published, at a fixed path, /.well-known/http-message-signatures-directory 19. The site receiving the request fetches the key once and checks the signature; the address the request came from no longer matters. Exa's page says its crawler does this and that user-agent strings "can be spoofed, so don't trust the string alone" 14. Fetched today, Exa's directory answers with one Ed25519 key (a signature algorithm) and is itself signed; so does the directory at chatgpt.com, one key, with a purpose field reading ai and an expiry a week out. Keenable's page says its requests carry no signature yet 13.

The protocol document is draft-meunier-webbotauth-httpsig-protocol, version 02 of 18 August 2026, an individual submission, expired and archived on the IETF's tracker 20. The keys are live; the standard that would make them portable is not finished. Cloudflare validates these signatures for sites behind its proxy and accepts either a signature or an address list as the proof for its verified-bots directory 21. The yes-or-no field that exposes the result to your own rules, cf.bot_management.verified_bot, "Requires a Cloudflare Enterprise plan with Bot Management enabled" 22. What every plan gets is AI Crawl Control, a dashboard of AI crawler activity, "Available on all plans" 23; the page does not say how it separates a verified crawler from a costume, so for a Worker of your own, the lists above are the check you can run.

What to do with a crawler log this week

  1. For each AI name in your logs, find it in the first table. A name with a list gets the checker; a name without one is a claim and stays labelled as one.
  2. Fetch the lists once a day. Five of the lists in the first table carry a date inside the last four weeks (Anthropic, ChatGPT-User, Perplexity's two, Googlebot's on 13 November); a list a month old misses new ranges and flags the crawler itself as a costume.
  3. Read the reverse DNS result only for Google, Bing, Common Crawl and the two partials; for the AI companies' addresses it says Amazon or Google Cloud, which is not an answer.
  4. A Signature-Agent header in a request is worth logging now, before it is common: today it names Exa or chatgpt.com, and the count of signed requests on your site is a number nobody has for you.

items.title: llama.cpp 1.0.0: 36 deprecated calls removed, --defrag-thold gone, FP8 KV cache on CUDA
items.summary: Out 13 November 2026, 10:20 UTC. Code on the old names stops compiling, a preset with defrag-thold stops the router, and -ctk f8_e4m3 halves the KV cache on NVIDIA GPUs. Homebrew still gives 0.9.0.
items.content_html:
llama.cpp, the program that runs open-weight language models on your own computer, published version 1.0.0 on 13 November 2026 at 10:20 UTC 1. The release page itself says one line, that a new version is out, with a note promising more at 15:00 CET; the notes are in the pull request that bumped the version, merged at 09:06 UTC 2. It is the first major version, and under the versioning rules proposed in the project's own discussion a major number means a break in the public library interface or the server's inference endpoints 19. Both happen here.

36 functions and one flag are gone from the header

The notes list the removal of llama_set_warmup, 35 deprecated functions, the defrag_thold field of the context parameters and the --defrag-thold command-line option 23. We read the two tagged headers on 13 November 2026: llama.h at v0.9.0 marks 36 functions DEPRECATED 4; at v1.0.0 none is marked and none of the 36 is declared 5. A deprecated function is one that still works but carries a warning naming its replacement; since 1.0.0 the compiler reports the old name as undeclared instead.

The 36 fall into five families, each with the replacement the v0.9.0 header names 4:

Removed, v0.9.0 headerReplacement
llama_load_model_from_file, llama_free_model, llama_new_context_with_modelllama_model_load_from_file, llama_model_free, llama_init_from_model
llama_n_ctx_train, llama_n_embd, llama_n_layer, llama_n_head, llama_n_vocabllama_model_n_ctx_train, llama_model_n_embd, llama_model_n_layer, llama_model_n_head, llama_vocab_n_tokens
llama_get_state_size, llama_copy_state_data, llama_set_state_data, llama_load_session_file, llama_save_session_filellama_state_get_size, llama_state_get_data, llama_state_set_data, llama_state_load_file, llama_state_save_file
llama_token_get_text, llama_token_get_score, llama_token_get_attr, llama_token_is_eog, llama_token_is_control, llama_token_bos, llama_token_eos, llama_token_eot, llama_token_cls, llama_token_sep, llama_token_nl, llama_token_pad, llama_add_bos_token, llama_add_eos_token, the six llama_token_fim_*, llama_vocab_clsthe same name with llama_vocab_ in place of llama_token_; llama_vocab_get_add_bos, llama_vocab_get_add_eos
llama_set_warmup, llama_sampler_init_grammar_lazywarm-up runs in your own code; llama_sampler_init_grammar_lazy_patterns

One grep finds every one of them in a code base:

grep -rnE 'llama_(load_model_from_file|free_model|new_context_with_model|n_(ctx_train|embd|layer|head|vocab)|(get_state_size|copy_state_data|set_state_data|load_session_file|save_session_file)|token_(get_text|get_score|get_attr|is_eog|is_control|bos|eos|eot|cls|sep|nl|pad|fim_(pre|suf|mid|pad|rep|sep))|add_(bos|eos)_token|vocab_cls|set_warmup|sampler_init_grammar_lazy)\s*\(' .

The same change promotes the NextN and speculative-decoding functions, 18 of them, from the private llama-ext.h into llama.h, and renames llama_set_embd_state_src to llama_set_ctx_state_src 23. Speculative decoding is the trick of letting a small draft model guess several tokens that the big model then checks in one pass.

--defrag-thold matters beyond C code. The server's router rejects a key it does not know in a --models-preset file, so a preset that still sets defrag-thold stops the router at start-up with an "option not recognized" error, as a comment on the pull request reports 3.

What stays: the llama_batch family. The v1.0.0 header still declares llama_batch_init, llama_batch_get_one, llama_decode and llama_encode next to the newer llama_batch_ext calls 5. A migration guide for it is an open pull request, and a reviewer there asked for a deprecation period before any removal 6.

Who is on the old header today

Anything compiled against llama.h by its old names: a C or C++ app, a Go, Rust, Dart or Swift binding, or a Python wheel that bundles the library. llama-cpp-python's newest wheel is 0.3.36 of 1 October 2026 7, and its main branch pins llama.cpp at a commit of 8 November 2026, four days before the prune merged 8, so it builds and runs today; the break arrives the day it moves its pin. Homebrew's formula is at 0.9.0 on 13 November 2026 9, which is the version brew install llama.cpp gives.

FP8 KV cache: 8 bits a value, the same perplexity as 8-bit blocks, CUDA for now

The KV cache is the model's memory of the conversation so far, so that each new token is compared against the old ones without rereading them; at long contexts it is the biggest thing in the GPU after the weights. Version 1.0.0 adds an FP8 cache, chosen with -ctk f8_e4m3 -ctv f8_e4m3, with optional static per-tensor scales 210. FP8 E4M3 is an 8-bit floating-point number with one sign bit, four exponent bits and three bits of mantissa. The list of cache types in common/arg.cpp at v1.0.0 now reads f32, f16, bf16, f8_e4m3, q8_0, q4_0, q4_1, iq4_nl, q5_0 and q5_1 12.

The q8_0 block is 32 signed bytes and one 16-bit scale, 8.5 bits a value; q4_0 is 32 four-bit values and the same scale, 4.5 bits 13. So FP8 saves 6% over q8_0 and half over f16, and what it buys is a format the GPU's tensor cores read directly rather than one the kernel has to decode first. The CUDA kernels came in on 11 November 2026, tested on an RTX PRO 4500, a Blackwell card 11. The author's quality table on that pull request, Wikitext-2 perplexity, where lower means the model predicts text better 11:

Model, 11 November 2026BF16 cacheq8_0 cacheFP8 E4M3 cache
NVFP4_fp85.45275.44915.4550
NVFP4_fp8_q85.47275.46415.4812

The three columns sit within 0.02 of each other. The notes name FP8 kernels for CUDA and say nothing about FP8 on Metal, Apple's GPU, so what -ctk f8_e4m3 does on a Mac is not in the release notes and not measured here. For an NVIDIA box serving long contexts, the move is one flag, and the memory comes back at the next restart.

The server refuses more by default

Four changes land for llama-server, the HTTP server most apps talk to 2:

  • With --tools or --agent, the web UI works on localhost by name or by its loopback number; any other host name on a loopback connection gets a 403. Behind a reverse proxy, --agent now needs --cors-origins set to the public origin, or the UI gets a 403. The fix closes DNS rebinding, where a page whose host name resolves to the loopback address could call /tools on a local server 14.
  • Tools or MCP on a --host that is not loopback, with no API key, refuse to start unless --allow-unauthenticated-tools is passed 15.
  • The CORS proxy no longer reaches local addresses at all, and a media URL on the LAN, a photo on a NAS for instance, needs --media-allow-private-urls 16.
  • HF_TOKEN goes only to huggingface.co hosts; a --model-url elsewhere no longer carries it, and MODEL_ENDPOINT is the explicit way to trust another host 17.

A cache for mixture-of-experts models with one GPU

A mixture-of-experts model uses a small part of itself for each token. When the experts do not fit in the GPU, 1.0.0 leaves them in system RAM, caches some on the GPU, and computes a share of the misses on the CPU instead of copying them over, set with --moe-cache-mib and --moe-cache-cpu-share; scripts/moe-cache-tune.py runs the server at several settings and prints the ones that fit the machine 18. The author's desktop example in the description runs at about 24 tokens a second with a 6,464 MiB cache and no CPU share, and at 83 with the recommended 24,000 MiB cache 18; commenters with other cards report smaller gains, and some report that a high CPU share slows a machine with slow RAM, so the script's numbers for your own box are the ones that count.

Getting it

The release page links the nightly build b12359 for binaries; the macOS arm64 archive is 16.9 MB 1. From source: clone, cmake -B build, cmake --build build --config Release, with Metal on by default on a Mac 20. The project's versioning discussion of 7 August 2026 describes weekly releases and semantic versioning, under which the next break of this size is a 2.0.0 19. Hongdam installs a local model and the server on a customer's own computer and pins the version that was tested 21.

items.title: Supabase CLI v3 is the default since 2 November: a CI db push now stops for a yes
items.summary: Since 2 November npm, Homebrew and the GitHub Action install Supabase CLI v3. Database commands target the local stack unless told --remote, and a hosted change fails without --yes where nobody can answer. Tested 10 November 2026.
items.content_html:
On 2 November 2026 Supabase released version 3.0.0 of its command-line tool, and from that day npm install supabase, Scoop, the Linux packages and the GitHub Action supabase/setup-cli install v3 when no version is named; Homebrew followed on 3 November 1. The CLI is the program that pushes database changes (migrations) to a Supabase project, deploys its edge functions (small server programs) and sets its secrets. Version 3.1.0 followed on 9 November 6. A deploy workflow that asks for latest got 2.122.0 on 1 November and 3.0.0 the next day.

Three changes stop a script written for v2 12:

  • Database commands target the local stack unless --remote is given. The local stack is the copy of Supabase that runs in Docker on the same computer. A db push in a CI job (continuous integration: the service that runs tests and deploys on each push, GitHub Actions for most) with no local stack fails. With one running, as in a test job, it pushes there and never reaches the hosted project 1.
  • A change to a hosted project asks for confirmation, default No. Where nobody can answer, the command fails with HostedMutationConsentRequiredError and changes nothing, unless --yes is passed. Piping y into the command no longer confirms it, and SUPABASE_YES in a .env file does not count 2.
  • Removed pieces fail outright. [inbucket] in supabase/config.toml stops supabase start; removed commands such as db remote commit and gen keys exit 1 and print their replacement 13.

Tested: the same push on v2 and v3, as a CI runner sees it

We installed supabase 3.1.0 and 2.122.1 from npm into separate folders, ran supabase init, added a migration file that creates a table, and started a throwaway Postgres on this computer to stand in for the hosted database. Every command ran with no terminal: input from /dev/null, output to a pipe, the way a GitHub Actions step runs. Measured 10 November 2026.

Commandv2.122.1v3.1.0
db push, not linkedProjectRefNotLinkedError, exit 1Target: local stack, then a connection error with the hint to start Docker, exit 1
db push --db-url $DB_URLapplies 3 migrations, asks nothing, exit 0a deprecation warning, then HostedMutationConsentRequiredError, exit 1, nothing applied
`echo y \db push --remote=$DB_URL`runs, with --db-url, exit 0the same error, exit 1
db push --remote=$DB_URL --dry-runlists the migrations it would apply, exit 0, no --yes needed
db push --remote=$DB_URL --yes"Confirmed by --yes", applies 4 migrations, exit 0
SUPABASE_YES=1 exported in the shell"Confirmed by SUPABASE_YES", applies
SUPABASE_YES=1 in .env, with or without the exportthe error, with "SUPABASE_YES in .env does not confirm hosted changes; pass --yes"
gen types typescript --localreads the local stacka warning that --local is not needed, reads the local stack
db remote commitRemovedSurfaceError, exit 1, "Use supabase db pull --remote instead"

The v2 row matters as much as the v3 ones. v2 asked its question only in a terminal; in a pipe it applied the migrations and said nothing. v3 refuses in the same place: "This run can't ask because stdout is not a terminal. Nothing was changed."

Run from inside an AI coding agent's shell, as we first did, v3 notices and answers differently: output switches to JSON and the error reads "This is an agent run: ask the user before re-running with --yes." An agent that runs the command gets that text instead of a prompt nobody sees 2.

Public workflows on GitHub: 4,728 run db push, 189 pass --yes

GitHub's code search over public repositories, read 10 November 2026 10. The counts are of files under .github/workflows and GitHub matches phrases loosely, so the figures move from day to day; the gap between the pairs does not.

version: latest is what Supabase's own CI examples use, on supabase/setup-cli@v1 78. The Action's README says @v1 installs CLI 2.20.3 when version is left out, and whatever latest means today when it is set 5. Today that is 3.1.0 6. The newest Action, @v3, reads the supabase version from package-lock.json, pnpm-lock.yaml or bun.lock at the repository root first, and falls back to latest 5. The two example workflows on Supabase's testing page, supabase db start and supabase test db, still run on v3, since both are local 8. The migration-deploy example already carries --yes --remote 7.

Lovable writes a project's migrations into supabase/migrations/ and applies them to the project itself, after you approve the SQL in chat 9. The CLI enters when the project is exported to GitHub and a deploy workflow is added, often written by the same tool that wrote the app. Those workflows are the 4,728.

The fix: the v3 forms, or a pin to v2

Moving to v3. Supabase's quick reference for CI, with the forms we tested 2:

v2v3
supabase db pushsupabase db push --yes --remote
supabase db push --db-url "$DB_URL"supabase db push --yes --remote="$DB_URL"
supabase migration list --linkedsupabase migration list --remote
supabase gen types typescript --project-id "$REF"supabase gen types typescript --remote="$REF"
supabase gen types typescript --localsupabase gen types typescript
supabase functions deploysupabase functions deploy --yes
supabase secrets set --env-file .env.productionsupabase secrets set --env-file .env.production --yes
`echo y \supabase <command>`supabase <command> --yes

A deploy step after the change:

- uses: supabase/setup-cli@v3
  with:
    version: latest
- run: supabase link --project-ref "$SUPABASE_PROJECT_ID"
- run: supabase db push --yes --remote
- run: supabase functions deploy --yes

--remote goes last when the command takes an argument, as in supabase migration repair 20240101000000 --status reverted --remote, or carries its value with =; otherwise the CLI reads the next word as the remote's name and stops with a "did you mean" error 23. The old flags --linked, --db-url, --project-id and --local still work in v3 with a warning and are removed in v4 2.

Staying on v2. The release of 2.122.1 on 2 November added install channels that stay on the v2 line 4:

- uses: supabase/setup-cli@v3
  with:
    version: v2.stable
"devDependencies": { "supabase": "v2.stable" }
brew install supabase/tap/supabase@2

v2.stable is a tag on the npm package, so npm install with that line in package.json installs 2.122.1 today and later v2 fixes; the release note gives the one-line form 4.

v2 now gets security fixes and fixes for broken behaviour, no features 4.

Either way. Rename [inbucket] to [local_smtp] in supabase/config.toml; v2.108.0 and later already read the new name, so the rename is safe before the upgrade 2. Run supabase db push --remote --dry-run in the workflow first: it lists what would be applied and needs no --yes, which we confirmed above. Two more v3 defaults reach production: secrets unset with no names fails and needs --all to remove every secret, and config push now applies [auth.sms] enable_confirmations = false as written, so supabase config diff before config push shows what will change 2.

items.title: GLM-5.3 Flash's replacements: Gemma 4 26B costs less per task, Qwen3.8 27B 3.6 times more
items.summary: Workers AI stops GLM-5.3 Flash on 20 November and names two small replacements. Ten builder tasks, two runs each: all four models 20 of 20 with thinking on; off, Gemma missed 2, Qwen 5. Both new ones run on the free allowance.
items.content_html:
Cloudflare's Workers AI stops serving GLM-5.3 Flash on 20 November 2026, and its deprecation notice names two small models to move to, Gemma 4 26B and Qwen3.8 27B, without saying which fits which job 1. We ran the same ten builder tasks on all three, plus GLM-5.3, on 9 November 2026: two runs per task, 180 calls in all. With thinking on, every model got 20 of 20. The difference is the bill. Gemma 4 26B used 410 neurons for its 20 runs, GLM-5.3 Flash 531, Qwen3.8 27B 1,920 and GLM-5.3 5,195. A neuron is Workers AI's billing unit across models; 1,000 of them cost US$0.011, and every account gets 10,000 a day free 2.

Two replacements named, and only the new ones run on the free allowance

The 5 November notice lists 16 language models that return HTTP 410 Gone with error code 5028 from 20 November, a date moved from 15 November 1. For the frontier end it points at DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM-5.3; for smaller jobs, at @cf/google/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it and @cf/qwen/qwen3.8-27b 1.

Model, price read 9 November 2026Input, US$ per million tokensOutput, US$ per million tokensOn the free allowance
GLM-5.3 Flash (ends 20 November)0.150.50No: paid plan or AI Gateway credits 23
Gemma 4 26B0.100.30Yes 2
Qwen3.8 27B0.453.20Yes 2
GLM-5.31.404.40No 26

The pricing page lists eight models that need a paid billing method; GLM-5.3 Flash and GLM-5.3 are on it, Gemma 4 26B and Qwen3.8 27B are not 2. A prototype that today needs a paid plan for GLM-5.3 Flash runs on the free 10,000 neurons after the switch. At the rate we measured, that is about 488 tasks a day on Gemma 4 26B with thinking on, or 104 on Qwen3.8 27B at its default.

Qwen3.8 27B is a dense model, one that uses all of its parameters for every token, with 27 billion of them 58. Gemma 4 26B is a mixture-of-experts model, one that uses a small part of itself for each token: 25.2 billion parameters in all, 3.8 billion active 7. GLM-5.3 Flash is the same kind at 320 billion total and 18 billion active 3.

With thinking on, all four answered 20 of 20

Thinking is the hidden reasoning a model writes before its answer. Workers AI returns it in a separate reasoning_content field and counts it in the output tokens it bills. A token is the unit a model reads and writes, about three quarters of an English word.

20 runs, model's default on Workers AICorrectOutput tokensSeconds, totalSeconds, medianNeuronsUS$ at list price
GLM-5.3 Flash, reasoning max2011,2611645.35310.0058
Gemma 4 26B, thinking on2014,56125611.64100.0045
Qwen3.8 27B, reasoning xhigh206,2902457.21,9200.0211
GLM-5.3, reasoning max2012,545873.35,1950.0571

Gemma wrote 29% more tokens than GLM-5.3 Flash and took 56% longer, and still cost 23% less, because its price per token is lower. Qwen wrote the fewest tokens of the four and cost 3.6 times what Flash did, because its output price is 6.4 times Flash's. GLM-5.3 was the fastest and cost almost ten times Flash.

The defaults differ. GLM-5.3 Flash and GLM-5.3 take reasoning_effort of low, high or max, default max, and their pages say reasoning cannot be turned off 36. Qwen3.8 27B takes low, medium or xhigh, default xhigh 5. Gemma's page lists reasoning as supported and names no default 4; in our 20 runs with nothing set, every reply carried a reasoning block, so Workers AI serves it with thinking on. Setting enable_thinking to true explicitly gave the same result, 20 of 20 at 12,094 tokens.

Thinking off cuts the tokens by 91 to 96% and fails the arithmetic

Both new models accept {"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false}} 789. Workers AI passed it through, and the replies shrank to a line.

20 runsCorrectOutput tokensSeconds, totalNeuronsWrong answers
Gemma 4 26B, thinking off186493430The 30-day token bill, both runs: 102.60 and 111.60 for 6.30
Qwen3.8 27B, thinking off1553931214Sundays in 2027 once (53 for 52), the three-server puzzle both runs, the token bill both runs (13.23 and 89.70)
GLM-5.3 Flash, reasoning low201,3103178none
Qwen3.8 27B, reasoning low205,1761891,586none

The code tasks, the SQL, the JSON and the cron line all passed with thinking off. What failed was multi-step arithmetic and the puzzle. GLM-5.3 Flash at low got all 20 for 78 neurons, the cheapest correct run of the day and a setting that goes away with the model. Neither replacement has a middle like it: Gemma is on or off, and Qwen at low still wrote four times the tokens of Flash at low.

For an app: leave thinking on for anything with numbers or conditions in it, and turn it off for extraction, formatting and short code, where it cut the Gemma bill by 93%.

The change is the model id and one field

import json, os, urllib.request

ACCOUNT, TOKEN = os.environ["CF_ACCOUNT_ID"], os.environ["CF_API_TOKEN"]
URL = f"https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/{ACCOUNT}/ai/v1/chat/completions"

def ask(model, prompt, thinking=True):
    body = {"model": model, "max_tokens": 8192,
            "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
            "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": thinking}}
    req = urllib.request.Request(URL, json.dumps(body).encode(),
                                 {"Authorization": f"Bearer {TOKEN}", "Content-Type": "application/json"})
    reply = json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=600))
    msg = reply["choices"][0]["message"]
    return msg["content"], msg.get("reasoning_content"), reply["usage"]["neurons"]

print(ask("@cf/google/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it", "How many Sundays are there in 2027? Number only."))

The usage block in every reply carries neurons next to the token counts, so a day's spend adds up from the replies themselves. For Qwen, reasoning_effort with low, medium or xhigh goes in the same body 5.

How we measured

Ten tasks a builder hands a model: a VAT total in baht, days between two dates, Sundays in 2027, a crontab line (the schedule format servers use), an SQL query (a question to a database) run against a test table, a Thai LINE order turned into JSON (data in labelled fields), a Thai national ID checksum function in Python run against test cases, a bug fixed in a Fibonacci function, a three-server logic puzzle with one solution, and a 30-day token bill. A script graded each answer: numbers compared, SQL executed, JSON parsed, Python run. Each task ran twice per setting, nine settings, 180 calls, through Workers AI's chat completions endpoint, four at a time, between 06:43 and 06:50 Bangkok time on 9 November 2026, with a reply allowance of 8,192 tokens and temperature left at the platform's setting. No call failed and none was cut off. Prices and neuron counts come from the replies and the pricing page of the same day 2; the 180 calls cost US$0.11 at list prices. The tasks are short, so the numbers say how the models spend tokens on small jobs, not how they do at long contexts. Hongdam picks the model for an assistant or a batch job by running the customer's own tasks this way 10.

items.title: The week: 16 Workers AI models end 20 November, Node.js patch day, Gemini 2.5 rerouted
items.summary: Six notes: a cache leak and its canary, npm install scripts, WordPress's update window, n8n 3.0, state tracking, Cloudflare's DNS scan. Plus five outside dates between 10 November and 2 December.
items.content_html:
On 5 November Cloudflare listed 16 language models that its Workers AI service stops serving on 20 November 2026. A request after that day gets HTTP 410 Gone (the status for an address that is gone for good) with error code 5028 1. Two of the 16, DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 and GLM-5.3 Flash, are the models measured in Monday's and Friday's notes below. That list leads the five outside dates. First, the week's six notes.

Six notes, 2 to 7 November

Monday, models. GLM-5.3 on Workers AI sent 155 replies with other customers' text: from 27 August to 9 September, Cloudflare's hosted GLM-5.3 answered 155 over-long prompts with text from other customers' requests, each with HTTP 200 and a token count that looked right. The engine had rejected the prompt on paper, the queue let it through, and the decode step read cache pages with earlier users' text still in them. Our canary test, hidden codes in a long prompt asked back, found 78 of 78 codes on three models up to 77,000 tokens for US$0.46. The code is in the note.

Tuesday, last-mile. Vercel now blocks bad npm packages; the npm in every Node LTS still runs install scripts: Vercel's build check, on since 2 November, reads the lockfile against a blocklist. The first install happens earlier, on the laptop or inside the AI tool, where npm 10 and 11 run a package's install script by default. Two lines in .npmrc, min-release-age=7 and strict-allow-scripts=true, tested on npm 10, 11 and 12; npm 10 ignores both and says so.

Wednesday, security. WordPress's upgrade-window flaw: partial updates carry no installer, full ones do: CVE-2026-119977, on CISA's exploited list since 3 November, is a race while WordPress unpacks a full update, when the staged copy's installer sits in a web-served folder for a few seconds. We opened the packages the update API serves: the automatic point update is about 50 files with no installer; a jump between branches unpacks 3,338. One server rule blocks the folder, and a fixed release exists for every branch back to 4.7.

Thursday, automation. n8n 3.0: npm installs end, Code nodes time out at a minute, no way back to 2.x: beta 27 October, stable due in early December. Self-hosted n8n needs Docker, a Code node task fails at 60 seconds instead of 300, unverified community nodes stop loading, 22 kinds of node vanish, and the database migration is one way. Every latest tag still served 2.46.6 on 5 November. The migration report under Settings lists the affected workflows today.

Friday, models. Running totals over 32 changes: 0 of 10 in one go, 10 of 10 writing each step: a small version of Ai2's StateBench on two open models. Values set once or overwritten came back right at every length; running totals and swaps failed in one go from 32 changes on and passed when the model wrote the values after each step, at 30 to 46 output tokens a change. For an app: log the value, not the change, or apply the changes in code and hand the model the result.

Saturday, last-mile. Cloudflare's DNS scan is a list of common names; generated DKIM names fall outside it: the quick scan matches record type and name against a list drawn from other zones, so Amazon SES's generated DKIM names fall through. A 92-query script asks Cloudflare's new nameservers before the registrar points at them and diffs against the old ones. The .com and .net registries let resolvers cache nameserver records for 48 hours, so the old host's DNS stays as it is for two days after the switch.

Five dates, 10 November to 2 December

20 November: 16 Workers AI language models stop answering. Cloudflare's list names DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731, DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813, GLM-5.2, GLM-5.3 Flash, Kimi K2.6, Kimi K2.7 Code, Nemotron 3 120B, QwQ 32B, Qwen3 30B and seven smaller Llama, Gemma and DeepSeek R1 distill models; eight image, speech, vision and embedding models go with them, each with a named replacement 1. The date moved from 15 to 20 November 1. Cloudflare's replacements for the language models: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM-5.3 for frontier work, Gemma 4 26B and Qwen3.8 27B for smaller jobs 1. On the pricing page, read 8 November 2026, the move from V4 Flash 0731 to V4.1 Flash 1017 lowers the price, US$0.44 to US$0.30 per million input tokens and US$1.32 to US$1.20 per million output; the move from GLM-5.3 Flash to GLM-5.3 raises it from US$0.15 to US$1.40 on input and from US$0.50 to US$4.40 on output, about nine times; GLM-5.3 Flash to Gemma 4 26B lowers it to US$0.10 and US$0.30 2. The model names above are the strings to search for in your code this week.

9 and 16 November, then 2 December: GitHub Actions blocks pull_request_target in public repositories. pull_request_target is a trigger that runs a workflow in the base repository, with the base repository's secrets, on a pull request from a fork 3. From 2 December GitHub blocks it by default in public repositories on Free, Team and Enterprise Cloud unless an Actions event policy allows it; private, internal and Enterprise Server repositories are not affected 3. Two brownouts, 9 and 16 November from 16:00 to 18:00 UTC, fail the runs the rule would block; between them the rule runs in evaluate mode and the Insights page shows what it would block 3. Enforcement was first set for 2 November 3. A policy can allow the trigger for named workflow files only 3.

11 November: Node.js security releases for 22, 24 and 26. The project's announcement, updated 3 November, puts the releases on or shortly after Wednesday 11 November, with the highest severity HIGH on each of the three lines 4. The newest releases today are 26.13.0, 24.22.2 and 22.23.4 5. Lines past their end of life get no release 4. A Dockerfile or a host that pins node:24.22.2 needs a new pin on the day.

1 December: Gemini 2.5 Pro and 2.5 Flash requests go to other models. Google's deprecation page, read 8 November 2026: from 1 December, API requests to gemini-2.5-pro route automatically to gemini-3.8-flash, and requests to gemini-2.5-flash to gemini-3.5-flash-lite, billed at the new model's rates 6. The code still runs and the answers change. The same page puts the Gemini 3.1 Flash TTS and Live previews and the 2.5 TTS previews at 17 November 6. A test set run against the new model name before 1 December shows what changes.

10 November: Supabase turns off four TLS 1.2 ciphers; CLI v3 runs locally by default. TLS is the encryption under HTTPS, and a cipher suite is one of the methods a client and server can agree on. Supabase removes the four CBC-mode TLS 1.2 suites from project HTTP APIs (Auth, Data, Storage, Realtime, Edge Functions) on 10 November; TLS 1.3 and the six remaining 1.2 suites stay, direct Postgres and pooler connections are not touched, and under 0.0001% of connections in the past 30 days used the removed ones, from end-of-life operating systems and embedded devices 8. The CLI's version 3, out 4 November, is the change more builders meet: db push, db pull, migration list, gen types and the storage commands target the local stack unless --remote is given, so a deploy script's db push can succeed on the laptop and change nothing hosted 7. Commands that change a hosted project ask for confirmation with No as the default and fail in CI without --yes; piped input no longer counts 7. Pinning the npm package to the v2.stable tag stays on v2, which gets fixes and no features 7.

items.title: Cloudflare's DNS scan is a list of common names; generated DKIM names fall outside it
items.summary: Cloudflare's quick scan adds records whose type and name match a list from other zones. Amazon SES's DKIM names are generated. A 92-query check before the switch, and the 48-hour registry TTL behind Cloudflare's 24 hours.
items.content_html:
Moving a domain to Cloudflare means changing its nameservers (the servers that answer where the website and the email live) at the registrar. Cloudflare offers to copy the existing records first, with a quick scan. Its reference page, read today, says what the scan is: a list of record types and names that recur across other zones (a zone is the set of records for one domain), matched against yours 1. It is not a copy of your zone. Records whose names exist only on your domain are the ones that fall through, and on a working domain those are mostly email records.

Yesterday we published a service that does this move with a check on both sides of the switch 10. This note is the reasoning behind that check, with the script and today's measurements.

The scan matches type and name, not your zone

Cloudflare builds the scan from pairs of record Type and Name that it sees in active zones 1. The content of the records plays no part, since content differs for every domain; a name like www or mail repeats across millions of zones, and that repetition is the list. The page gives the pairs it usually finds: an A record at the apex (the bare domain), a CNAME or A named www, an MX at the apex, a CNAME named mail, an A named webmail 1.

The same page names what the scan does not find: a hostname specific to one zone, its example my-store1900, and a DKIM record under a custom name, its example this._domainkey where default._domainkey would be found 1. Cloudflare's setup page puts the consequence in one line: review the apex, www and the email records yourself before changing the nameservers 2.

The full list of names is not published. Whether a fixed name such as google._domainkey is on it is unknown; the page says only that custom names are expected to be missed.

Which mail providers use fixed names, and which generate them

DKIM is a signature on outgoing mail; the receiving server checks it against a public key published in your DNS under <selector>._domainkey.<domain>. The selector is the provider's choice.

ProviderRecord nameTypeFixed or generated
Google Workspacegoogle._domainkeyTXTFixed default prefix google; a different prefix can be typed in 3
Microsoft 365selector1._domainkey, selector2._domainkeyCNAMEFixed, the same for every organisation 4
Amazon SES, Easy DKIMthree records, each <token>._domainkey, the page's example abc123._domainkeyCNAMEGenerated per domain and per AWS Region 5
Resend, measured on motdang.net todayresend._domainkeyTXTFixed

A generated token appears in no list of common names, so the three SES records fall outside any scan built the way Cloudflare describes. Microsoft's two fixed names may or may not be on the list; Cloudflare's page does not say. Microsoft's page says signing of a custom domain starts once it detects the two CNAME records in DNS 4. A DKIM record that did not come across leaves receivers unable to check the signature; whether the mail still arrives then rests on the SPF record and the domain's DMARC policy.

Ask Cloudflare's nameservers before the registrar points at them

Cloudflare assigns two nameservers when the zone is created 2. A query sent to one of them by name is answered from the new zone, whichever nameservers the registrar still lists. That allows a comparison before the switch: snapshot what the old nameservers answer, ask the two new ones the same questions, and diff.

Our script does that 6. It asks 92 questions per domain: the apex and www as A, AAAA and CNAME; mail, webmail, smtp, imap, pop, autodiscover and autoconfig; the Outlook _autodiscover._tcp SRV; the apex TXT (where SPF lives), _dmarc, _mta-sts, _smtp._tls; and 32 common DKIM selectors, each as TXT and as CNAME. It also asks the registry (the operator of .com, .net or another ending) for DS records, the sign that DNSSEC (signatures on DNS answers) is on.

python3 tools/dns_move_check.py before example.com
python3 tools/dns_move_check.py compare example.com <ns1>.ns.cloudflare.com <ns2>.ns.cloudflare.com
python3 tools/dns_move_check.py after example.com

compare exits 1 on any mail record that differs. Website records are allowed to differ, since Cloudflare's proxy answers them with its own addresses. Measured 7 November 2026 from Chiang Rai, one run per domain, on four domains already on Cloudflare:

motdang.net
Questions asked92
Records found8
Of which mail4: MX, SPF in the apex TXT, _dmarc, resend._domainkey
DKIM selectors answering, of 321
Time4.0 s

The other three domains took 2.8 s to 4.0 s each. The limit is the one the scan has, in smaller form: a DKIM name outside the 32 is not found by asking. The SES tokens, the one case where the name cannot be guessed, come from the provider's settings page, and that page is read for every domain regardless of what the script finds.

Mail hosts stay DNS only

Only A, AAAA and CNAME records can go through Cloudflare's proxy; MX and TXT are always DNS only 7. The proxy answers web requests; a mail host whose A record is proxied answers with Cloudflare's own addresses 9, and Cloudflare's email-records page shows that host as DNS only in its example and says port 25, the mail port, is not proxied by default 8. One more rule from the proxy page: when one A record on a name is proxied, every A record on that name is treated as proxied 7. The quick-scan page does not say which proxy status it sets on what it finds; the orange cloud beside each mail host is read after the scan.

Cloudflare's 24 hours, the registry's 48

Cloudflare's setup page says to wait up to 24 hours while the registrar updates the nameservers, that online checkers lag because they use cached results, and to confirm with dig ns <domain> @1.1.1.1 2. The 24 hours is the registrar's side. On the other side sit the resolvers (the servers that look names up for phones and laptops), and they cache the old delegation for the registry's TTL, the time-to-live on the record. Measured today at the registries' own servers:

For a .com or .net domain that is 48 hours. Four public resolvers asked for one of our .net domains today reported remaining TTLs of 86,252 s (Cloudflare's resolver), 86,400 s (OpenDNS), 43,200 s (Quad9) and 21,600 s (Google Public DNS): what each reported as remaining, lower than the registry's figure and none below six hours. A resolver that looked the domain up just before the switch answers the old nameservers until its copy expires, so the old host's DNS stays as it was, records intact, for two days after the switch, and the old hosting is cancelled after that, not on the day.

Once the zone is on Cloudflare, later changes move faster: proxied records carry a fixed TTL of 300 seconds, and Auto on an unproxied record is 300 seconds too 9.

Order of the day

  1. Create the zone, run the scan, then read the mail provider's settings page and add every record named there, SES tokens included 15.
  2. Run before against the old nameservers and compare against the two new ones; a GAP line is a record to add 6.
  3. DNSSEC off at the registrar if before printed DS records; Cloudflare's page says changing nameservers with it on can make the domain unreachable 2.
  4. Change the nameservers; dig ns <domain> @1.1.1.1 until it answers the new pair 2.
  5. Run after, send one mail from the domain to an outside inbox and read its authentication headers, and leave the old host's DNS alone for two days.

items.title: Running totals over 32 changes: 0 of 10 in one go, 10 of 10 writing each step
items.summary: Ai2's StateBench paper says language models lose values that change over a long text. In our small version on two open models, set and overwritten values came back right; running totals and swaps only with every step written.
items.content_html:
Asked for the end of a running total after 32 changes, DeepSeek V4 Flash got 0 answers right in 10. Told to write the values after every change, the same model got 10 of 10. We measured this on 6 November 2026 on two open models on Cloudflare Workers AI, with a small version of StateBench, a test that three researchers at Ai2 (the Allen Institute for AI) published on 2 November 2026 12.

StateBench tests state tracking: a model reads a list of changes and says what each value is at the end. In the paper, Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna did well when values were set or overwritten. On running totals and swaps they did no better than guessing once inputs reached 10,000 to 64,000 tokens 1, and scored 13% or lower on the longest swap problems 2. A token is the piece of text a model reads or writes: a word, part of a word, or one character. Our logs are far shorter: 115 to 7,263 tokens.

Two kinds of change are look-ups; two need every line

The paper sorts changes into four levels 1. Our test has four kinds of line; in a shop's message log they look like this:

KindA line in our testIn a shop
Set oncea <- 7; and the same line again lateran order number
Overwrittena <- 3;"the delivery address is now…"
Running totala <- (a + 3) mod 10;"add two more bags"
SwapTMP <- a; a <- b; b <- TMP;two guests trade rooms

mod 10 drops the tens, so each value stays one digit. For the first two kinds, one line answers the question: the last line that names the variable. For the last two there is no such line. Each change builds on the one before, and a reader that skips one ends on the wrong value.

The paper's hardest level is a chain of swaps among five values 12. An earlier paper by the same three authors argues that a transformer (the design behind today's language models) reading its input in one pass cannot solve it 4. Our swaps use four variables, which the paper's maths places one level lower, beside running totals. The one-go answers failed there all the same.

Our test follows the paper's design: one random sequence written four ways, with the same variable changed at the same position in each 3.

In one go: look-ups right, the rest guessed

DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 answers without thinking first; each reply was 13 tokens. Whole answers right, out of 10:

Kind8 changes32128512
Set once10101010
Overwritten1010108
Running total9000
Swap0110

From 32 changes on, 8 of its 120 running-total values were right; picking digits blind gets about 12. On swaps, 31 of the 38 wrong replies gave the right four values in the wrong places; 7 of those were the starting values, untouched. A wrong reply has the same form as a right one: a=5 b=7 c=4 d=0.

Written steps get it right, at 30 to 46 output tokens a change

A model gets room to work in two ways: the prompt tells it to write the values after every change, or the model thinks before it answers, writing working that is billed as output tokens. GLM-5.3 Flash thinks unasked. Theory backs both: a transformer allowed to write a number of steps in proportion to its input's length can, on paper, do every task of this kind 5.

Whole answers right, of 108 changes32128512
Running total, DeepSeek writing steps1010102 of 3
Swap, DeepSeek writing steps101071 of 3
Running total, GLM thinking1099not run
Swap, GLM thinking10102; 7 timed outnot run

The room is paid for in output tokens: about 30 per running-total line and 46 per swap on DeepSeek, 60 and 77 in GLM's thinking. On the two look-up kinds GLM, thinking, got 80 of 80 right.

At Workers AI's prices on 6 November 2026 (DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731: US$0.44 per million input tokens, US$1.32 per million output 6), one log of 128 swaps cost US$0.0008 to answer in one go and US$0.0086 with written steps, and took 55 seconds in place of 1.

Three things went wrong as the logs grew:

  • The model stops writing steps. Two of the three wrong 128-swap answers opened by saying the list was long, then wrote only the two values each swap touched. At 512 swaps one reply skipped the steps altogether.
  • Values appear twice. All three wrong 128-swap answers named one value twice (a=3 b=4 c=3 d=4). No chain of swaps does that.
  • The call runs out of time. Every call still running at about 235 seconds came back as HTTP 408, "Request timeout": 15 of GLM's 18 calls on 128-swap logs (7 logs timed out twice) and one of DeepSeek's three 512-change running totals. The limits page gives no time limit; it gives 20 requests a minute for each paid model on standard billing 7.

For an app that reads a log

  1. Log the value, not the change. "Stock: 7" in place of "sold 3" turns a running total into an overwrite, which the one-go model answered right 30 times of 30 up to 128 lines.
  2. Apply the changes in code and hand the model the result:
def apply(state, e):
    if e["do"] == "set":  state[e["key"]] = e["to"]
    if e["do"] == "add":  state[e["key"]] += e["by"]
    if e["do"] == "swap": state[e["a"]], state[e["b"]] = state[e["b"]], state[e["a"]]
    return state

state = {"bags": 2, "room_101": "guest A", "room_102": "guest B"}
for e in events:              # each message that changes the order
    state = apply(state, e)
prompt = f"Current order: {state}\n\nCustomer: {last_message}"
  1. Where the model has to read the changes itself, ask for the values after each one, allow 50 output tokens per change, and check the answer in code. After swaps the same set of values comes back; a reply with a value twice is wrong.

Hongdam sets up chat assistants that answer from your own pages 8.

Run it yourself

import random
VARS = "abcd"

def problem(kind, n, seed):
    r = random.Random(seed)
    st = dict(zip(VARS, r.sample(range(10), 4)))
    lines = [f"{v} <- {st[v]};" for v in VARS]
    for _ in range(n):
        t, s = r.sample(VARS, 2)
        delta, const = r.randint(1, 9), r.randint(0, 9)
        if kind == "once":
            lines.append(f"{t} <- {st[t]};")
        elif kind == "overwrite":
            st[t] = const
            lines.append(f"{t} <- {const};")
        elif kind == "increment":
            st[t] = (st[t] + delta) % 10
            lines.append(f"{t} <- ({t} + {delta}) mod 10;")
        else:
            st[t], st[s] = st[s], st[t]
            lines.append(f"TMP <- {t}; {t} <- {s}; {s} <- TMP;")
    return "\n".join(lines), st   # the text for the model, the right answer

The one-go prompt: "Track the current value of each variable after executing the assignments in order. TMP is a scratch variable." then the lines, then "Reply with only the final values of a, b, c and d, in this form and nothing else: a=_ b=_ c=_ d=_". The written-steps prompt swaps the last sentence for "Work through the assignments one at a time. After each one, write the current values as a=_ b=_ c=_ d=_ on a line. Then end with one last line in this form: FINAL a=_ b=_ c=_ d=_".

How we measured

Four variables with digit values, four lines that set them, then 8, 32, 128 or 512 changes. Ten random sequences per length, each written the four ways; three per kind for written steps at 512. We read the last a=_ b=_ c=_ d=_ in each reply and counted an answer right when all four values matched. Models: @cf/deepseek-ai/deepseek-v4-flash-0731 and @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3-flash through Workers AI's chat endpoint on 6 November 2026, temperature left at the platform's setting. Reply allowance: 512 tokens for DeepSeek in one go, 8,192 with written steps (28,000 at 512 changes), 32,768 for GLM. That is 366 prompts, 358 of them answered. Calls refused with HTTP 429 were sent again, and the GLM calls that timed out were sent once more. Our counts are of 10, and we did not test the paper's four models.

items.title: n8n 3.0: npm installs end, Code nodes time out at a minute, no way back to 2.x
items.summary: The n8n 3.0 beta came out on 27 October 2026, stable due in early December. Self-hosted n8n must run in Docker, unverified community nodes stop loading, and a Code node task fails after 60 seconds instead of 300.
items.content_html:
n8n (a workflow automation tool you can run on your own server) released version 3.0.0 as a beta on 27 October 2026, with the stable release due in early December 2. The breaking changes are mostly removals and tighter defaults 1. Three of them stop workflows on the day you upgrade: self-hosted n8n must run in Docker (software that packages a program with everything it needs into a container), a Code node task fails after 60 seconds instead of 300, and community nodes not verified by n8n stop loading 1. There is no path back to 2.x once the database has migrated 29.

The 2.x line gets security fixes and fixes for serious bugs for 12 months after the stable 3.0 release. The 1.x line ends on 31 December 2026, and a 1.x instance has to go through 2.x first 2.

The npm path ends, and it already broke once this week

n8n 3.0 does not publish a runnable package to npm (the package registry for JavaScript). An instance started with npm install -g n8n or npx n8n cannot move to 3.0 as it is; it needs Docker first 1. Kubernetes and Helm installs (cluster deployments) are not affected 2.

The npm path is fragile before 3.0 arrives. From 2.46.0 the package refused to install on any machine with an "unsupported platform" error, because the new Edit Image node shipped four platform-specific image libraries as regular dependencies and no host matches all four 5. 2.46.4 went out as the stable release on 2 November with the fault in it; 2.46.6 fixed it on 4 November 45.

n8n's replacement is a one-line installer, curl -fsSL https://get.n8n.io | sh, which checks for Docker and the Compose plugin, writes an .env and a Compose file, and starts the instance 1. We read the script on 5 November 2026 (version 1.4.0, 577 lines) 6. It asks GitHub for the latest stable release and pins that version in .env; the script's own comment says a floating tag would upgrade and run database migrations on any container restart 6. It also starts a separate sandbox service for running code, pinned at 1.8.1 6. On failure, and only after you answer yes at a terminal, it sends n8n the script version, the OS name and the failed step 6.

Twenty-two kinds of node vanish, and their workflows do not start

A workflow that uses a removed node fails when it runs. A published one does not activate when 3.0 starts, so its triggers stop firing 1. The list runs to 22 entries, several naming more than one node: the legacy Function and Function Item nodes (replaced by the Code node), Item Lists, Cron and Interval (replaced by Schedule Trigger), Read PDF, Read and Write Binary File, the legacy OpenAI node and OpenAI Assistant, HTTP Request Tool, Workflow Trigger, the Insert and Load variants of the Pinecone, Supabase and in-memory vector stores, and the AI Transform node 1.

Version 1 of the AI Agent node goes too, with its SQL, Conversational, OpenAI Functions, Plan and Execute and ReAct modes; the current version replaces them all with Tools Agent 1. Edit Image versions 1 and 1.1 go, and version 2 uses a different image library, so blur, text placement and PNG quality can come out differently 1.

The migration report can rewrite some of these for you: Cron to Schedule Trigger, AI Transform to a Code node holding the same generated JavaScript. It saves the result as a new workflow version, and the published version keeps running until you publish the new one 3.

Three defaults shrink, one credential gains a required field

Setting2.x default3.0 default
N8N_RUNNERS_TASK_TIMEOUT (Code node task)300 s60 s
N8N_COMPRESSION_NODE_MAX_DECOMPRESSED_SIZE_BYTES2 GiB256 MiB
N8N_COMPRESSION_NODE_MAX_ZIP_ENTRIES5,0001,000
N8N_UNVERIFIED_PACKAGES_ENABLEDtruefalse

From the breaking-changes page, read 5 November 2026 1. Each old value can be set back by hand in the environment.

A Code node that calls a slow API, or loops over a few thousand rows, now fails at the minute mark 1. Unverified community nodes (packages from npm that n8n has not reviewed) cannot be installed after the upgrade, and the ones already installed stop loading, unless N8N_UNVERIFIED_PACKAGES_ENABLED=true is set 1.

The Slack API credential requires a signing secret (a value from your Slack app's settings that lets n8n check each incoming request came from Slack). A workflow with a Slack Trigger does not publish without it, and an already published one does not activate after the upgrade 1. The secret sits under Basic Information in the Slack app settings and goes into the credential's Signature Secret field 1.

Two more changes catch instances with custom settings. The binary data folder inside n8n's data directory is renamed from binaryData to storage on first start, and 3.0 refuses to start when both folders exist 1. The in-memory binary data mode is gone; instances still on it switch to filesystem, which needs disk space on the container's mounted volume 1.

Every "latest" still points at 2.x today

Measured 5 November 2026, 06:40 in Chiang Rai:

ChannelWhat it serves
npm latest and stable2.46.6, no 3.x version published 7
Docker Hub latest and stable2.46.6 8
Docker Hub next and beta2.47.2 8
Docker Hub 3.0.0, 3.0.1, 3.1.027 October, 28 October, 3 November 8
GitHub "latest" releasen8n@2.46.6, so the one-line installer installs 2.46.6 today 46

3.0.0, 3.0.1 and 3.1.0 are marked pre-release on GitHub 4. To run the beta, name the tag: docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n:3.1.0. No floating tag serves 3.x today.

The order of work

The migration report, at Settings > Migration Report on 2.39 or later, scans the instance and lists each affected workflow with its owner, its node, its run count and the date of its last run 3. Five impact levels sort the work: Upgrade blocked, Executions will fail, Executions might fail, Behavior changes, Capability removed 3. A workflow that has not run in 12 months gets a banner offering to mark it won't fix 3.

  1. Update to the newest 2.x. In Docker that is the stable tag; by npm, 2.46.6 or later 45.
  2. Open the report. Fix Upgrade blocked and Executions will fail first, then the rest 3.
  3. Add the Slack signing secret, set N8N_RUNNERS_TASK_TIMEOUT if any Code node runs longer than a minute, and decide on each unverified community node 1.
  4. Back up the database. The 3.x migration is one way 29.
  5. Upgrade a copy first, then the live instance 2.

An npm install needs the Docker move before step 5. The one-line installer starts a new instance rather than converting the old one, so the old instance's workflows come across by export and import: the editor's Import from File, the CLI or the API 1.

For a founder

If someone set up n8n for you with a single npm command on a small server, the December release is the one your instance cannot take. The report in Settings tells you, today, how many of your workflows will stop. A morning of fixes on 2.x now beats a silent stop in December.
